Interestingly, we discover that this charged sphere has a surface energy comparable to that of the droplet model, despite being made up of individual particles, each with positive energy, yet collectively displaying an increase in energy that cannot be explained by energy addition in the overlap region.

Lerman's work on symplectic reductions and WKB approximations has yielded a broader theory involving symplectic modifications. This paper will build upon Lerman's findings, incorporating his method of geometric microlocal analysis to examine symplectic reductions in greater detail. By extending Lerman's techniques, we will derive formulas for calculating local symplectic modifications, reducing higher-order symplectic structures through iterative applications of lower-order reductions.

This research introduces a new entity suggestion approach for Wikipedia-based applications, leveraging the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph. Unlike existing methods, our approach uses an innovative two-layer embedding technique. First, we create a hierarchical diagram to illustrate relationships between categories of Wikipedia entities. Each category is represented as a connected component of approximately 100 linked Wikipedia pages. Secondly, we craft a more precise diagram to showcase intricate connections within each individual page. Using the structured relationships in these diagrams, our approach outperforms the current entity suggestion benchmarks.

Living donor kidney transplantation offers seropositive recipients matched with seropositive donors few options for compatible kidneys. Despite sharing the same antibody issue, these pairs may still face rejection if they do not achieve ideal acceptance. Current research assumes pairs will always achieve ideal acceptance, but in reality, this is not always the case. In this study, we introduce a Markov decision process model to examine the decision to accept an incompatible kidney offer. Our analysis of the model's equilibria provides insights into the behavior of seropositive donor-recipient pairs making kidney transplantation decisions, with implications for policy makers aiming to increase the rate at which these pairs agree to ideal acceptance.

We uncover both explicitly stated and implicitly understood connections between topics in mathematics that are central to an important research area.  Implicit Connections was created to provide a clear path for graduate students to explore the underlying mathematics behind algebraic and geometric topology through the study of applied areas.  As such, the course has demonstrated its value to multiple students, leading to several notable research contributions.  To further achieve its purpose, we have made the materials used in Implicit Connections freely available on an open platform, making it accessible to a wider audience and providing an example of collaborative learning in mathematics.

Our analysis reveals that many variations of word representations, including those derived from neural networks, frequently misclassify words from the Loughran-McDonald dictionary, which has become a widely used benchmark for identifying the grammatical complexity and negativity of words. We examined twenty-seven different word representation models and seven corresponding reduction techniques, but unfortunately found that none of these models performed exceptionally well, with a top model achieving only a 0.25 improvement in accuracy over a random guess. We also discovered that the primary source of this difficulty lies in the diverse nature of semantic evaluations, which cannot be accurately captured through a single-dimensional polarity score. We propose enhancing word representations with a dimension that considers grammatical complexity in addition to negativity, and provide examples of improved performance using multiple evaluation metrics and real-world financial applications.

This article proposes a novel approach to fully integrate information and energy transfer in wireless communication systems.  A key concept is the idea that the real part of the received signal can be used for energy harvesting, in addition to utilizing the imaginary part for information transfer.  By formulating the received signal in terms of its real and imaginary components, we derive a key equation and demonstrate its implications for both energy and information transfer.  To facilitate easy integration, we separate the transmit and receive signals into independent real and imaginary parts.  However, this approach leads to interchannel crosstalk in SISO and MISO systems.  To rectify this issue, we adopt an alternative method based on the received signal's real and imaginary parts.  Specifically, we represent the received signal in the form $y_k = \sum_{i=0}^{K-1}s_i \, e^{j2\pi k i}$, where $y_k$ can be used for both information decoding and energy harvesting.  To eliminate crosstalk in SISO and MISO systems, we apply a new precoder and decoder design that takes advantage of the phase information.  Theoretical gain improvements, in the order of $10\log_{10} K$, are demonstrated and verified through simulations with both AWGN and fading channels.  The results demonstrate that our approach yields significant performance enhancements in terms of spectral efficiency and energy transfer efficiency.

This research introduces a novel method to model the interaction between melting fluids and solidifying solids. By combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques, our approach leverages the strengths of both methods to address challenges arising from interface singularity and advection-diffusion equations. Utilizing a fixed grid approach for both the level-set function and the solution fields, our model facilitates seamless integration with conservative finite difference schemes, enabling an efficient and stable numerical implementation. To validate our method, we have simulated numerous scenarios, including stationary melts under external forces, heat applied to the edge of a solid, and a solid undergoing phase change, and compared our results to established methods and theoretical predictions.

We present a novel application of unary connectives in language, drawing from ideas in supervaluationism and the bucket approach to tense and modality. Our system builds upon classic logical frameworks using unary operators, superposition, and interference. A key feature of our system involves assigning unary modal operators to single words in a sentence, unlike traditional applications that treat them as scope. Our approach allows for the expression of complex relationships between words and incorporates an interpretation method using our logical system's built-in features. Furthermore, our system facilitates the evaluation of sentences with overlapping scopes through the adoption of a quantum interpretation method.

We develop a novel approach to a longstanding challenge in game theory: identifying a player's most preferred equilibrium strategies that are consistent with their observed partial feedback in multiplayer symmetric competitions. By leveraging the player's observed payoffs and strategies from a limited number of past encounters, our approach pinpoints a specific set of rationalizable equilibria. The efficiency of our approach is demonstrated to depend on the player's ability to accurately model the payoffs and minimize the deviation of the observed strategies. The effectiveness of our approach is guaranteed to yield at least one rationalizable equilibrium strategy for the player, and potentially multiple strategies may satisfy this condition. The execution of our approach is computationally feasible and can be implemented using standard optimization algorithms. The breadth of our results is showcased through the derivation of corresponding Theorems 1-4, addressing specific scenarios and providing the best known guarantees to date for a significant category of games.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model on a dynamic graph is conducted, focusing on a specific mechanism where node connections change to reduce disease transmission. As the graph evolves, a key metric of interest is the number of active individuals. A theoretical framework is established to study the model's dynamics and assess its impact on epidemic spread under various conditions. A critical threshold is identified, where a significant increase in the rate of connection changes accelerates epidemic spread. Further, a more pronounced effect of changing connections is found to hinder epidemic spread, although this requires careful consideration of graph connectivity.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, we demonstrate that when the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, a nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold with a specific metric can support Cotton solitons.

A theoretical foundation for adjusting PDFs within the NNFFNNSiLoVanDamme framework has been established. This framework effectively combines the neural network and Abelian effective field theories approaches to describe PDF evolution through diffusion and splitting processes. A key aspect of this foundation is the incorporation of neural network predictions for global summary quantities of data sets, comprising lattice data, heavy and light particle experimental outcomes, and Higgs mass measurements. This framework provides a solid theoretical basis for adjusting PDFs using neural network predictions of global quantities and an input weight that determines the neural network's influence according to x-value.

To accelerate policy updates in reinforcement learning, experience replay has been a widely used technique by reusing previously collected data. Despite its benefits, the standard implementation of experience replay remains limited due to the random selection of transitions, which does not take into account the unique characteristics of the policy being optimized. To overcome this limitation, we propose a data-efficient experience replay method that chooses samples based on the reduction in estimated variance of policy value estimates. By minimizing the variance, our approach effectively reduces the expected difference between the sampled policy values and the target policy, thereby facilitating more efficient policy updates. Our evaluation across multiple benchmark tasks demonstrates the superiority of our method over random sampling and other reinforcement learning benchmarks.

We introduce libcommute, a cutting-edge C++11/14/17 and Python 3 library that leverages the power of computational symmetry to efficiently create custom Hamiltonians and perform precise, hybrid diagonalization across a range of applications. By employing operator algebra language, libcommute provides a flexible and concise framework for users to define their spin, fusion, and multiplicity patterns, thereby streamlining the specification of symmetry-related properties. These features are complemented by a user-friendly interface and a range of tools for numerical simulations, phase transition analyses, and topological physics investigations.

By integrating scanning transmission electron microscopy and theoretical modeling, our study discloses the intricate internal architecture of BaFe$_2$As$_2$-type superconductors and reveals diverse FeAs layering, including the previously unexplored "rotated-tetragonal" phase. Our findings also reveal various void shapes within hexagonal voids, demonstrating a strong correlation with the onset of superconductivity. Our proposed model highlights the crucial role of voids in influencing the material's self-assembled lattice, and potentially its superconducting properties.

We've derived two advanced Hubbard-Stratonovich transformations - the generalized HS and superbosonization equations - and demonstrated they lead to equivalent results for specific applications. Our analysis reveals the superbosonization equation can be derived from the generalized HS formula and vice versa, depending on the variables being transformed. Both equations possess similar Gaussian matrix input requirements and produce similar quadratic non-commutative matrix equations from their respective quadratic input precursors.

To study top quark polarization in the t-channel single top quark production process, we have analyzed three different observables and examined how well they can differentiate between the helicity configurations of the top quark and its counterpart, the W boson. The choice of observables is based on properties of the spin density matrix and was tested using the PyTTH event generator with the CTEQ6M parton distribution functions. The evaluation was performed at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Future Circular Collider (FCC) to cover a range of center-of-mass energies from 8 to 100 TeV. The results show that the littlecross and kappa* observables demonstrate a clear energy dependence at all LHC energy levels, offering a promising avenue for investigating top quark polarization. Furthermore, the fudge factor is also examined to ensure the accuracy of these findings.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the metallic state in a LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattice using NMR with a focus on spin diffusion and the temperature dependence of the Knight shift. By examining $^8$Li NMR spectra within LaNiO$_3$ layers, we found the Knight shift to be directly proportional to temperature, displaying similar behavior to other itinerant electron systems. Additionally, we observed that the Knight shift's temperature dependence becomes more linear with increasing temperature. Spin diffusion measurements revealed a temperature-independent spin diffusion rate, consistent with the zener model using the LaAlO$_3$ layer's direct exchange interaction. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the metallic state in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices.

In our research, we introduce MultiTalk, a diverse dialogue system that effectively handles numerous topics. Unlike other approaches that focus on combined questions and lengthy continuing conversations between multiple participants, MultiTalk is designed to manage a wide range of topics, including personal stories, personal opinions, and personal experiences. Its unique feature is its extensive branching, meaning that the dialogue can take on many different paths. To achieve this, we developed a large, combined text dataset that integrates numerous sources, consisting of over 1 million items, to use as training data. To build the dialogue system, we employed a set of simple, integrated techniques, including bidirectional neural methods for generating responses and evaluating conversations. To test the system's performance, we created various evaluation metrics and methods, including human assessors who evaluated its understanding, coherence, and overall quality. The results showed that MultiTalk's coherence and overall quality scores were significantly better than other approaches on both automatic and human assessment. Furthermore, we found that certain features, such as the number of paragraphs, the length of the input, and the type of topic, had a notable impact on the conversation's quality.

Our research is focused on enhancing the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, utilizing intelligent surface technology and multiple input and multiple output devices, and investigating how correlated signal transmission and a non-linear signal phase shifting method impact performance. By mathematically modeling correlated signal transmission and using a non-linear signal phase shifting method represented by a Gaussian distribution, we develop a novel approach to determining the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system. To evaluate system performance with correlated signal transmission and using a non-linear signal phase shifting method, we conduct a quantitative analysis, and find that correlated signal transmission and using a non-linear signal phase shifting method can significantly increase the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system. Furthermore, our research finds that introducing an intelligent surface can substantially increase the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, especially in scenarios with high transmission frequency correlation. Moreover, we identify transmission frequency bands with optimal performance, and demonstrate that an intelligent surface can increase the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system by optimizing signal transmission direction.

We've developed a new method for adapting N-body simulations in altered gravity theories, and have successfully applied this technique to a range of cosmological scenarios. Using a simplified model based on a conformally coupled quintessence field, we created a new potential function that maintains the fifth force's kpc-scale characteristics. Our approach enables us to conduct a full N-body simulation in an altered gravity environment using an N-body simulation in a standard gravity setup, allowing us to leverage existing well-tested N-body codes with only minor adjustments. By comparing our method's results with those from bespoke N-body simulations, we confirmed its effectiveness for predicting galaxy positions, masses, and spin axes. Our technique should significantly expedite the development of high-resolution N-body simulations for a broad spectrum of altered gravity theories.

Researchers discover that conformal field theories with central charge $c=1$ contain subsets of multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) driven by stochastic log-gases evolving on the upper half of the complex plane. Specifically, they show that for $k$ distinct points $x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_k$ in the real line, the Gaussian free field defined on the Euclidean unit disk $D$ and restricted to the Schramm-Loewener curve $\gamma_{\kappa_1}(x_1) \cup \cdots \cup \gamma_{\kappa_k}(x_k)$ has a well-defined and unique measure. This finding can also be applied to obtain multiple SLEs for $k \geq 2$. Furthermore, it has been found that the conformal field theory with $k$ marked points $x_1, \ldots, x_k$ can be obtained from the fusion of two theories defined on marked points $x_1, \ldots, x_{k/2}$ and $x_{k/2+1}, \ldots, x_k$.

MediaWiki-based platforms like Wikipedia have a proven track record of effectiveness in the development of high-quality knowledge projects, especially when multiple authors collaborate. WorkingWiki is an innovative tool that builds on this success by transferring the strengths of MediaWiki to a research environment. It offers a versatile framework where a diverse range of data types, including statistical software output, experimental data from sensors, and computational results from remote servers, can be integrated with ease. WorkingWiki enables seamless real-time collaboration among researchers, with features like instant commenting and secure editing controls. By providing a robust wiki structure, WorkingWiki aims to revolutionize the way collaborative research is managed, similar to the impact seen with wiki-based approaches to documentation.

This research aims to analyze the interaction between a turbulent jet flame and a structure experiencing acoustic vibrations in a confined space. Acoustic waves generated by the flame's instability can lead to flame oscillations and subsequent heat damage to nearby structures. In response, flame stabilization techniques have focused on reducing flame instability through increased airflow speed. However, instead of relying on airflow speed, this study investigates the effect of acoustic vibrations on flame shape and heat release rate. A numerical model was developed to simulate flame behavior and heat release rate under both local flame instability and fully developed turbulent flow conditions. Results showed that acoustic vibrations caused symmetric flame shapes to become asymmetrical, leading to increased heat release rates. However, in cases of pre-existing asymmetry, heat release rates decreased due to the formation of recirculating flow patterns, reducing the risk of heat damage to nearby structures.

The acoustic modes in a star are a combination of oscillations in pressure and density.  As the frequency increases, the motion shifts from being primarily a change in pressure to a change in density, with a significant change in geometry.  This work re-examines the identification of gravitational modes in stars, particularly for high-frequency oscillations in density and the associated geometric modes.  It includes a mathematical derivation of the conditions for a non-zero gravity mode and the associated mode eigenfunctions.  Our analysis shows that the condition of a non-zero gravity mode is not met for typical stellar models, with estimates suggesting it would require a star mass of around 10,000 times the mass of the Sun.  A new approach is presented to derive the geometric mode eigenfunctions directly from the dispersion equation.  This method is shown to be more efficient than the standard approach and may provide benefits for computational stability.

A novel technique for finding clusters of synchronized neurons and a specific type of phenomenon called traveling chimeras in neural networks has been developed. Traveling chimeras occur when some neural cells are synchronized and produce action potentials in a specific pattern, while others remain inactive, and this pattern moves through the network. This technique, based on linear algebra, can provide detailed information about the structure of synchronized groups. To work effectively, the technique requires that the neural connections within the network do not change over time. To detect traveling chimeras, the technique is applied to a specific snapshot in time. The development of this method facilitates a more systematic exploration of spiking neural networks.

In this study, atoms or molecules closer together (in a two-dimensional intermolecular continuum model or a two-dimensional Ising model with adjacent site interactions) are more likely to cluster together, with this tendency increasing with the strength of intermolecular interactions. This effect is more pronounced in the case of hard particle interactions. Analyzing these scenarios with regular and irregular lattice structures, our research shows that stronger intermolecular interactions cause a greater shift towards clustering, with a more significant impact when particles can get very close to each other.

In encounters between neutrinos and ultralight dark matter, we examine how neutrino non-standard interactions are influenced in a quantum gravity microcosm, where standard model degrees of freedom coexist with ultralight scalar field dark matter. By relating the neutrino non-standard interactions to the primordial lepton asymmetry, we find that significant dark matter density can cause the disappearance of beta beta decay involving a neutrino and an antineutrino. This process's suppression has observable consequences for stellar light curves following supernova explosions and influences the rates of certain rare nuclear decay processes. Furthermore, we show that primordial lepton asymmetry, born out of the interactions between neutrinos and dark matter in supernovae, has implications for the rates of certain rare nuclear decay processes and affects the energy released in type II supernovae explosions, potentially slowing down the spin of a protoneutron star through electromagnetic processes until it can start rotating rapidly.

The concept of UHE photons is simulated in a paper by M. B. Smirnov and G. B. Smirnov, originally published in Astroparticle Physics, considering a hypothetical scenario in which extremely energetic photons are produced at the Sun due to a hypothetical process occurring within the Sun's core. It is assumed that these photons have energies exceeding $10^{20}$ eV and are directed towards the Earth, possibly resulting from a process such as pair production using a field that is significantly stronger than typical magnetic fields in the Sun. The simulation models a hypothetical, isotropic stream of UHE photons and their interactions with the Sun's magnetic field, focusing on how this interaction affects their direction. The simulation shows that in a scenario where the magnetic field strength is consistent with observations, most photons will not have their direction significantly altered as they approach the Earth. However, in a scenario where the magnetic field is stronger than observed, a significant number of photons will likely have their direction altered in a way that would cause them to miss the Earth. The simulation also indicates that in a scenario where the magnetic field is stronger than expected, a significantly smaller fraction of photons will fail to have their direction significantly altered as they approach the Earth. We're exploring a novel nonlocal gravitational concept based on an emergent gravity framework, where spacetime's geometric structure is redefined through interconnections between physical fields that propagate similar nonlocal patterns. Our analysis focuses on a simplified model where a nonlocal scalar field represents the primary gravitational effect, incorporating a local degrees-of-freedom within it. We've established that this nonlocal gravitational field obeys an equation derived from an emergent gravity theory, proving it results in a modified Einstein field equations when the nonlocal field is closely related to the local one. We also discovered that this nonlocal modification leads to a linearized equation resembling the Fierz-Pauli action. Furthermore, we've identified that the nonlocal gravitational field introduces an infinite number of conserved quantities, including angular momenta, linear momenta, and an energy related to the conformal factor of spacetime. We've also leveraged a technique called "constitutive calculus" to analyze the nonlocal gravitational field's constitutive properties, revealing how the nonlocal field responds to external linear stress tensors that may lead to the formation of dark matter and dark energy phenomena.

In distributed and replicated databases, updates can conflict, leading to issues with data consistency. To address this, user applications must be designed with specific rules in mind to ensure that updates don't result in conflicts. These rules, however, should focus solely on preventing conflicts and won't be concerned with achieving any particular level of data consistency. Users need to adhere to these rules to ensure the replicates remain conflict-free, allowing for efficient handling of updates across the replicated databases. Building on previous work, we introduce an innovative approach, Eliminate-Win, an efficient design for handling conflicts in replicated data forms. This approach can serve as a foundation for designing applications that replicate data across multiple systems, providing a straightforward and effective means of preventing conflicts.

To gain a deeper understanding of the interactions between genetics and environment in human traits, we are inviting researchers to cooperate on a range of health-related areas. For this purpose, we are offering users the option to publicly share and explore their GWAS and functional genomic data. Users can browse the available datasets, which include annotations for 18 different conditions and 2 GWAS datasets. Additionally, our platform allows users to visualize and mine their own data using a range of tools, including enrichment analysis, network exploration, and track views. To facilitate collaboration, we are introducing a new feature enabling multiple users to work together on the same project. This enables multiple experts to jointly interpret GWAS data, including functional genomic elements, gene expression, and chromatin conformation data, as demonstrated by the inflammatory bowel disease example provided. This tool also facilitates the exploration of GWAS data from a computational perspective, with options to run custom scripts and make direct queries to the underlying database.

This paper discusses the interconnection between Little Hierarchy and Little Slittings in the context of the Standard Model, its minimal supersymmetric extension, and a supersymmetric model with a limited number of Higgs singlets. We examine the capabilities of present and future particle colliders to discover or verify the theories underlying Little Hierarchy. The focus lies on recently proposed detector concepts and potential advancements in detector technology that could enhance the sensitivity to Little Hierarchy. A previously overlooked, potentially significant effect has also been identified, which may have a notable impact on the interpretation of experimental findings.

Reanalyzing 13 years of data from the RXTE and Swift satellites for a specific group of neutron star binary systems that shine with X-rays, we have observed that the time between some of their X-ray bursts is not random but rather consistent with a specific pattern. Furthermore, this pattern typically lasts for several months to a few years before the X-ray bursts become randomly distributed again. Additionally, the time it takes for the X-ray bursts to return to the same pattern varies significantly, ranging from as short as two years to over a decade. Comparing our findings to previous research, we have found that the group's behavior we studied is unique. Considering that all these neutron star binaries are located within the Milky Way and that their X-ray patterns change over time, it's difficult to determine if any specific neutron star binary system is currently exhibiting a pattern in its X-ray bursts. Therefore, we cannot accurately identify all the neutron star binaries that are active in the galaxy. Based on data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, we have found that the majority of neutron star binaries within the center of the Milky Way do not regularly shine with X-rays, suggesting that many of these systems are not actively producing X-ray bursts due to the orbit of their companion star blocking the X-rays.

A binary system composed of compact stars serves as the most sensitive laboratory for testing general relativity's validity, given its extreme conditions of high gravity and fast motion.  While combining general relativity with an equation of state for dense matter resolves most issues, nuances in the matter's nature still have a significant impact.  Recent research into neutron star properties using electromagnetic observations from mergers has somewhat constrained possible matter behavior.  However, many possible states of matter continue to exist, still allowing for distinct differences in binary system observations.  Key features of these possible matter states will need further, independent confirmation through multiple tests, involving binary systems of different components and in various states of motion and interaction, in order to settle the issue of matter's nature and binary system behavior as predicted by general relativity.

We analyzed radio sources at a frequency of 1.4 GHz using data from the VLA Low-frequency Survey. By examining sources with flux densities between 1.4 and 2.4 Jy, we found minimal variation in the properties of compact radio sources with angular sizes, except for sources larger than approximately 0.3 mas. These larger sources, which are likely to be weak-line or broad-line Type 1 Active Galactic Nuclei, show a higher ratio of linear to circular polarization and a longer projected linear size when viewed edge-on. The higher polarization ratio in these sources may indicate a relationship between the unusual structure and the polarization properties. Additionally, sources with larger angular sizes have a more collimated radio source morphology, characterized by a higher ratio of major to minor axis. This could imply that radio sources with larger angular sizes have undergone more significant interaction with their surroundings, influencing their shape and orientation.

We analyze three distinct scenarios of massive stellar explosions - a Type II supernova, a stellar collapse explosion, and a massive star eruption - to determine if a shockwave forms as a result of a dense matter jet produced by core accretion or a magnetar formed in the star's core. If a shockwave is generated in these explosions, as in supernovae of Type II, it will have a similar speed to that of supernovae and be directed at a similar angle at the star's equator. However, in contrast to supernovae, the shockwave in these explosions is powered by the energy released as the explosion interacts with the surrounding star tissue, rather than the expansion of the shockwave itself. This difference in energy source affects the temperature distribution within the shockwave. In a Type II supernova, the temperature of the shockwave reaches as high as 10 eV (about 20,000 Kelvin or 36,000 degrees Fahrenheit) at a distance of about 10,000 astronomical units from the star. In a stellar collapse explosion or a massive star eruption powered by a magnetar, the temperature of the shockwave is lower, at around 5 eV (about 10,000 Kelvin or 18,000 degrees Fahrenheit) at the same distance.
