In recent years, X-ray-based weapon detection has gained significant attention due to its potential to enhance public security in airports, subway stations, and office buildings. In an effort to enhance detection effectiveness and system practicality, researchers have focused on combining artificial intelligence with baggage scanning systems. Although various studies have utilized deep learning models to analyze X-ray images, a lack of high-quality benchmarks has hindered comparison and collaboration. To address this shortcoming, we've developed the initial publicly accessible dataset and evaluation protocol for X-ray-based weapon detection, comprising 10,000 images divided into training and testing sets of 5,000 each. Our innovative approach involves integrating a deep learning model with a unique filter to suppress irrelevant information, enabling the system to focus on distinguishing between weapons and neutral objects. Compared to existing models, our network achieved the best balance of precision and efficiency in identifying banned items in low-light conditions.

We've developed a quantum invariant, referred to as $Z_{K}$, for chains positioned within the thickened torus $T^2 \times I$ in $S^3$. This invariant exhibits marked volume hypothesis behavior, serving as a key precursor to the development of a bounded-coherent version of the intersection form for chains within this topology class. The construction of $Z_{K}$ involves combining the Kauffman bracket skein module of $T^2 \times I$ with a specific linear functional, termed $K_{\tau}$. By establishing the marked volume hypothesis behavior of $Z_{K}$, we've also demonstrated the existence of locally rigid configurations, or relative equidistant chains, for finite numbers of spheres within $T^2 \times I$.

Context-gloss enhancement is proposed as a method to improve Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). A context-gloss pair is classified into one of the target sense labels for a given polysemous word. Our approach builds upon existing strong baselines by utilizing Bidirectional Transformers for Inter-sentence Context and Gloss to enhance the classification performance. The evaluation of our approach on four WSD data sets for the task of context-gloss classification has shown positive outcomes. Moreover, our approach has achieved superior performance on three out of four WSD data sets when compared to the state-of-the-art approaches in Word Sense Disambiguation. The code for the proposed context-gloss enhancement approach has been made publicly available at https://github.com/lyosong/Context-gloss-Enhancement.

Helmholtz-type integrals of the reciprocal Gamma function have been established in a previous study, and this work builds upon that result. By transforming the original Gamma function using the change of variable formula, new hyper-singular and singular integral representations of the reciprocal Gamma function are derived. Specifically, a second type of hyper-singular integral representation is obtained for the negative integer values of $x$, and a singular integral representation is derived for non-negative integer values of $x$. These new formulations hold promise for deriving alternative representations of other special functions and potential applications in numerical boundary element methods.

In proton-proton interactions at the LHC, detecting the top quark's production is straightforward due to the long lifetime of the top quark, which allows for clear identification of its decay products. Conversely, identifying the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus interactions at the LHC will be a more complex task. Given the small mass difference between the W and top quarks, their decay products, in particular the electrons and muons, are sensitive to the mother particle's mass. Within the PHOSIA experiment, we aim to reconstruct top quark production events in proton-lead interactions by analyzing the invariant mass spectrum of electron and muon pairs. Our approach involves selecting events containing high-energy leptons with low momentum transfers, which significantly reduces background contributions. By integrating signal and background event yields over appropriate ranges, we can determine the sensitivity of our reconstruction to the top quark mass. Our findings will facilitate the design of more intricate experiments, such as those involving heavy ions, which will be crucial in detecting top quark production at the future LHC runs with enhanced sensitivity.

This study introduces a novel data-driven approach to text-to-SQL parsing across domain boundaries, leveraging a supportive task to facilitate learning. By positing that each database table holds distinct patterns of query history, we develop a proprietary dataset to train a model using a classification approach. To overcome the challenge of scarce training data for multiple domains, we employ transfer learning and mix-matching techniques. The supporting task helps the primary parser model to learn by utilizing shared pattern features. Our results indicate that combining data from multiple domains enhances parsing performance, with a notable 25% improvement in F1 score compared to single-domain training. Furthermore, our proposed approach achieves a 10% increase in F1 score on the target domain with limited training data, outperforming existing multi-domain approaches.

Machine learning models relying on structured data have seen remarkable success in various applications. The underlying data structures commonly used are graphs, which pose significant challenges for current ML technology due to their intricate and dynamic nature. Despite these difficulties, researchers have achieved impressive results in training ML models with structured data using techniques such as node classification and link prediction through the application of neural network models and differential privacy. This article provides an in-depth review of the state of the art in differential privacy for graph-organized data used to train ML models, examining existing research, pinpointing existing shortcomings, outlining promising avenues for further exploration, and offering guidance for potential contributors in this field.

As the largest digital archive of paintings ever created, the collection from the Photonic Survey Instrument for Art History and Education will offer significant opportunities for research in the field of science. By analyzing images taken at a wavelength of 1060 nanometers, which passes through glass and reflects light from pigments on walls, researchers can investigate topics such as varnish preservation, wall surface changes, and the detection of pigments. In addition, they will gain valuable insights into the performance of the PSI system and its imaging technology.

In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate challenging road networks for evaluating the navigation capabilities of autonomous vehicles. Our approach uses a set of control points to define a complex area, from which a specific route is calculated. To create multiple road networks, we employ various methods to systematically alter the control points, leading to multiple potential routes within the complex area. Our approach enables us to systematically analyze different road networks by controlling the complexity of the evaluation environment. Additionally, we used this approach to evaluate the navigation capabilities of an existing algorithm in the context of complex road networks.

Melody captioning is an innovative task that requires identifying the text that best matches a song's melody. In this research, we introduce a related yet distinct task called music description, which involves generating text to accompany a musical playlist. Unlike conventional song descriptions that focus on existing lyrics, this task aims to create original descriptions tied to specific melodies. Building on the framework established for melody classification, our model incorporates attention mechanisms to improve performance. We also introduce a novel metric to evaluate music description coherence and present models that integrate with the attention-based framework, leading to enhanced results. Although significant challenges remain in this area, our work lays the groundwork for future exploration in this field.

Quantum hydrodynamics has proven an invaluable tool for modeling the dynamics of quantum many-body systems by linking their microscopic properties to macroscopic hydrodynamic behavior. Building on this concept, we develop a random quantum hydrodynamics framework that accounts for both interactions and random phase-space fluctuations in Bose gases. This approach enables us to simulate the experimental observation of a Bose condensate and investigate the effects of impurities on a dilute Bose gas in one dimension. Our model demonstrates that interaction and randomness effects become indistinguishable and can be described by a single combined parameter. Furthermore, we find that certain impurity patterns can create spatially separated phases of the Bose gas, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding hydrodynamics in interacting, imperfect quantum fluids and potentially extending the application to other interacting, dilute gases in one dimension.

Understanding temporal activity patterns in video is a challenging task, and a key aspect is identifying context that aids in differentiating short-duration action segments from background. Current approaches tend to focus heavily on feature extraction but give less consideration to context modeling. In response, we introduce a dual context network for activity detection, seeking to extract both action and background contexts, then combining them to classify segments into background or forward to action detection. Through dual context fusion, our model refines the extracted contexts, integrating them into a robust learning framework. Experimentation with SCTV and MVTec datasets demonstrates our dual context approach to enhance temporal activity context, achieving superior performance compared to straight feature extraction. Code is available at https://github.com/ghr1202/Dual-Context-Net-for-TAD.

This work focuses on an exotic feature of edge current density, called Palm Tree Modes (PTM), observed in the JET tokamak. PTMs were initially discovered in 2011 as unusual, asymmetrical patterns appearing in the outer peddle of plasma current measurements. Unless addressed, these modes can lead to edge localization and subsequent plasma disruptions. This study aims to provide a theoretical framework for understanding and identifying the underlying causes of PTMs. It suggests that these modes may arise from a specific interaction between the plasma edge and the scrape-off-layer, fueled by a particular type of Eddy in the tokamak's divertor chamber. A key finding suggests that the traditional condition for PTMs, involving a specific relationship between the strike point and the edge current, may not be universally applicable. Instead, this study reveals that a more critical factor is the presence of a particular type of flow in the divertor, which can vary depending on the location within the chamber. It also proposes a method for predicting the occurrence of PTMs based on the location of the plasma interaction area and the flow profile in the divertor. This research used data from the JET and MAST tokamaks, although the underlying theory has yet to be thoroughly tested against these datasets.

This research focuses on preventing collisions among autonomous robots moving autonomously in a space, with an emphasis on dynamic scenarios. Our approach utilizes a vector field method, introducing a potential field that dynamically changes in response to the robots' movements. A key aspect of this method involves analyzing how the field's gradient affects the robots' path, resulting in a derivation of a critical distance for collision avoidance. To enhance efficiency, this distance is optimized through adjustment of the field's curvature, ultimately yielding an optimal value. Our collaborative collision avoidance protocol leverages this understanding to manage the robots' movement, achieving a balance between preventing collisions and minimizing detention time. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in managing complex robot interactions.

In independent trials where the outcome can be any nonnegative real number, a fundamental asymptotic result known as the law of large numbers holds. It expresses that the average of many independent trials will, on average, be close to the actual averages of these trials. A more precise result, known as an extensive central limit theorem, provides a specific measure of how the average of many trials deviates from the actual average. It has been extensively researched and its conditions well characterized for sequences of independent trials. However, the conditions for trials that are not independent are less well understood, especially in cases where the conditions are closely related, such as seeing letters in random sequences, like the letters E, F, G in scientific notation, or letters in the alphabet's second half. This paper investigates the conditions under which the standard extensive central limit theorem applies to these types of dependent trials, and it finds that certain deviations can occur frequently, or in a nonnegligible way, which significantly restricts the possible conditions for trials that are only slightly dependent.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the potential benefits of intelligent reflective surfaces to enhance and control wireless signal patterns. By adjusting their reflections, these surfaces can influence local maxima of signal reception patterns and optimize communication link performance. This research introduces a novel concept where a intelligent reflective surface interacts with radar technology to improve target parameter estimation. By optimizing reflection patterns, the surface can increase the distinctiveness of received signal data, facilitating more accurate target parameter estimation. A benchmark solution based on maximum contrast ratio methods is established and a more effective algorithm is developed to minimize contrast ratio function constraints. Numerical analysis and simulations demonstrate the enhanced performance of the new algorithm in estimating target parameters.

Comparing the efficiency of different fuzzers is a challenging task due to the diverse output coverage metrics used in each one. Most contemporary fuzzers rely on coverage-based evaluation, often incorporating features like AST analysis to enhance their effectiveness. A key shortcoming of existing fuzzer assessment techniques is their inability to compare fuzzer performance across various applications, largely because of the wide range variations in output formats and coverage definitions across different software. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to evaluating and differentiating fuzzers, introducing a unified standard for assessing fuzzer performance, as well as a versatile testing framework to facilitate reproducible experiments and easy adaptation to new targets. Our evaluation of multiple state-of-the-art fuzzers on various programs has yielded valuable insights, revealing that the performance of these fuzzers can vary significantly, depending on factors such as program characteristics and properties. Our research has significant implications for the software vulnerability discovery field, emphasizing the importance of considering delivery, exploration, and failure aspects in the evaluation of fuzzers. To support the community in developing and comparing future fuzzers, we have openly shared our evaluation framework, results, and data, in the interest of advancing the field through collaborative research efforts.

Interventions during ongoing learning pose several challenges, including the potential for negative effects on previously acquired knowledge. This phenomenon is not well understood in research on ongoing learning, which is being driven by the increasing availability of continuous learning datasets. This research is being led by the few studies that can handle the temporal structure of sequential data. A new benchmark designed for ongoing learning challenges the effectiveness of models that utilize pre-trained networks, specifically those that can process visual and linguistic information. When tested on a series of images that change over time, this model struggles to recover from setbacks, with its performance declining to below chance levels. In contrast, the model performs well on standalone images. This discrepancy highlights the limitations of models that utilize pre-trained networks in situations that require them to manage changes over time.

This work proposes a new concept of weakly local minimizers for regions in a metric space with varying dimensions, building on the principles of geometric measure theory. We establish that these weak local minimizers possess stable points of minimal density and characterize the homotopy type of the stable set. Notably, in Euclidean space, we define an analogue of minimal surfaces that is not necessarily embedded and determine the stable set's homotopy type based on the fundamental group of the boundary.

This final installment builds upon previous research concerning the extended-time behavior of solutions to semilinear parabolic equations with convergent initial conditions, specifically when the equation has an unstable critical point. Previous findings addressed cases where the equation had a stable focal point and had been recently expanded to cover focal and elliptic points. This study further broadens its scope to encompass all types of singular points found in first-order ordinary differential equations, thereby demonstrating that solutions converging to singular points eventually converge to the shorter, non-trivial limit cycle between them.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus using the monopole tensor interaction part of the Fujita-Miyamoto interaction, a multi-Interaction Shell Model, have led to a notable finding. In this case, a normal and reverse pair coexist in a stable manner at the null spin point, a condition rarely found in other nuclei. Further research has been conducted to explore other possible interactions that could achieve this unique configuration. Using the Monte Carlo shell model, it was found that only the monopole tensor interaction and a specific combination of the Fujita-Miyamoto interaction can achieve this coexistence at the null spin point. Characteristics of this coexistence, such as pair density and single particle energy, have been analyzed to gain a deeper understanding.

In recent years, research on finding equilibria in online learning has been focused on the fewest possible number of questions needed to be asked, known as inquiry complexity. This study aims to explore the minimum inquiry complexity required to achieve an equilibrium by querying an unknown environment, with specific attention being given to environments that change over time and affect player incentives. Under certain conditions, it has already been established that the minimum inquiry complexity for reaching an $\epsilon$-approximate equilibrium in multi-action, multi-player games is $O\left(\frac{d^2}{\epsilon^2}T\right)$, with parameters $d$ representing the dimensionality of the action space and payoffs, $\epsilon$ indicating the margin of error, and $T$ denoting the number of time steps. This research further refines that result by relaxing certain conditions and considering more permissive frameworks, with specific findings including: - In positive-paying multi-action games without time variation, the lowest inquiry complexity for achieving an $\epsilon$-approximate equilibrium is $O\left(\frac{d^2}{\epsilon^2}T\right)$. - In negative-paying multi-action games without time variation, the lowest inquiry complexity for achieving an $\epsilon$-approximate equilibrium is $\Omega\left(\frac{d^2}{\epsilon^2}T\right)$. - In multi-action games with time variation, the lowest inquiry complexity for achieving an $\epsilon$-approximate

Machine learning models are often assessed using techniques from mathematics, specifically those from the field of probability, statistics, and geometry. Despite being widely employed, k-fold cross-validation remains poorly understood among machine learning practitioners. This knowledge gap persists, even among those who use and train models for more than a decade. Here, we clarify how averaging results from k-fold cross-validation can be calculated using simple arithmetic, and we show that using a larger k minimizes the uncertainty when comparing models of equal complexity. Our explanation is mathematically rigorous and free from statistical jargon. We also explore how the choice of k influences the comparison of neural networks with similar parameters, a question that has been debated on internet forums. Our findings can help those working with machine learning codes, like Hugging Face's Transformers, by providing them with a data-driven approach that compares models for language understanding tasks.

Recent advancements in semantic technology have been accelerated by the abundance of educational resources available online. One area that has gained significant attention is the automatic creation of concept bases from online course materials. In this context, instructional graphs have become a popular tool for modeling knowledge, with various approaches emerging to build and manage them. This article provides an in-depth review of relevant research strategies, emphasizing various challenges that arise when working with educational datasets, particularly regarding entity types, relation characteristics, and proposed solutions. Furthermore, our discussion covers existing evaluation metrics, testing methodologies, and the limited availability of gold standard datasets for evaluation. To address this limitation, we present a novel approach to assessing the quality of concept bases, along with a proposed framework for validating them.

We introduce a novel, efficient algorithm for finding exact MPE (Minimum Possible Evidence) solutions in graphical models, specifically Bayesian networks and Markov domains. Our approach splits into two parts: first, rapidly identifying a high-quality approximate solution using a heuristic function, and second, refining this estimate through precise search within a constrained space. The boundaries of this search space are determined by the initial approximation, ensuring it contains the exact MPE solution. We demonstrate that our algorithm yields exact results for MPE when the initial approximation matches the solution, and test it against other exact and heuristic methods for finding MPE in sample Bayesian networks and image scenes. The results show our algorithm typically requires significantly fewer queries to produce an exact MPE solution compared to other exact methods. The code for the algorithm is included with this submission.

We investigated the impact of photon recoil on absorption spectroscopy using an ultracold strontium vapor and a single-beam setup, comparing our findings to both theoretical predictions and a conventional two-beam method. By analyzing the effects of photon recoil, we determined that it results in a significant increase in absorption minimum depth, differing greatly from the two-beam approach. Furthermore, the influence of photon recoil was found to vary based on the angle between the vapor cell and the laser beam, influencing the accuracy of our measurement in the one-beam setup. A correction for this factor was derived and demonstrated to be essential for obtaining reliable, photon-recoil-free data in the one-beam setup.

The shear thinning behavior of complex fluids leads to an unusual transition as flow rate increases, where the fluid's viscosity suddenly drops exponentially in a narrow range. This phenomenon is well observed but not well understood in bulk measurements, which are Complicated by measurement tools and sample conditions. We studied this transition using advanced imaging techniques in a microfluidics setup, which allows for precise temperature and wall conditions. Our research discovered that this exponential drop in viscosity occurs when flow rate changes are scaled in proportion to the rate of shear strain, which is a measure of flow intensity. This finding provides a new framework for analyzing this exponential drop in viscosity.

The Racah algebra is a lesser-known extension of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ that contains elements commonly found in both the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and the braid algebra associated with the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. By examining a specific subgroup of the Weyl group $W$ acting on the Dynkin diagram of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, we can identify a family of algebras known as the Racah algebras. A particular subgroup of the Weyl group $W$ that stabilizes the Dynkin diagram of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ generates the Racah algebra, and this algebra has been shown to contain a specific sequence of Hilbert-Poincaré series that cannot be found in either the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ or the braid algebra associated with the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. By exploring the stabilizer subalgebras defined by the subgroups of the Weyl group $W$ that stabilize the Dynkin diagram of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, we can determine a relationship between these algebras and the central extension of the braid algebra associated with the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$.
