Investigating the thermodynamics and near-extreme Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes under scalar field perturbations can provide insight into the feeble cosmic censorship hypothesis, which suggests that singularities in general relativity are concealed behind horizons except in specific, perturbatively accessible scenarios. In this study, researchers examine how the scalar field affects thermodynamic properties and the nature of the singularity. They discover that, regardless of the field's strength, the singularity remains inaccessible and that the scalar field has no noticeable impact on the entropy or temperature near the horizon. However, the scalar field does cause fluctuations in the position of the event horizon's inner edge, effectively creating a "barrier" that singularities must cross in order to become observable. This finding implies that the presence of a scalar field violates the equality part of the weak energy condition but maintains the positivity part, and that the field may lead to the emergence of a Gravitational Repulsive Effect (GRE).

In 1921, Ernst Zermelo introduced the axioms of set theory, which has become the foundation for numerous mathematical theories. Over time, some of these axioms have been identified as insufficient and new ones added, such as the Axiom of Choice in 1922 and Foundation in 1922-1923. Our research proposes the addition of three novel axioms to the ZF framework, drawing from the paraconsistent and paracomplete approaches to logic. By integrating these axioms into the standard schema of set theory, we demonstrate that they do not contradict the existing axioms and do not lead to absurd consequences. Our proposed theory, PFZ, offers a framework that avoids the problems associated with naive set theory, such as the Russell paradox, and enables the construction of sets containing contradictory or complementary elements. Furthermore, PFZ facilitates the development of sets with rich properties, such as those necessary for the theory of real numbers and model theory.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces and signal processing technology enable the continuous analysis of brain signals to estimate key parameters of a person's movement, including walking speed and stride length. Our research builds upon this by introducing a novel method to forecast ambulatory states and stride frequency from local electrical brain activity measured via an electrocorticogram, a direct reading of brain electrical activity. Our approach combines artificial neural networks with spectral features from continuous, 64-channel ECoG signals, successfully predicting ambulatory states and stride frequency in both healthy individuals and stroke patients who have undergone surgical brain implantation. The results demonstrate accurate predictions when using real-time data, indicating potential for the development of a brain-based system to monitor patients' rehabilitation progress during ambulatory activities outside of a controlled laboratory setting.

This paper introduces a new computational approach to estimating the entropy of diverse probability distributions by leveraging the Nested Sampling method. Initially developed for evaluating expectations in complex scenarios, our proposed algorithm builds upon this framework to calculate integrals related to entropy formulas, ultimately yielding an efficient entropy estimation technique. By harnessing the power of Nested Sampling, our approach enables us to efficiently evaluate entropy quantities even when dealing with highly intricate probability distributions that cannot be easily managed through conventional analytical methods. To illustrate the benefits of this approach, we demonstrate its application by estimating entropy measures for both simple and complex examples, including distributions of random matrices, and intriguing scenarios of random fractals, showcasing notable time complexity improvements over traditional methods.

Minimally generated finite groups that contain no copies of A times the cyclic group Z have no nontrivial subgroups containing elements of infinite order. We employ this property to create a new class of groups that cannot contain nontrivial finite subgroups. By combining it with the property of being minimally generated, we obtain a new class of groups that cannot contain nontrivial finite subgroups and cannot contain elements of infinite order within any of their proper subgroups. We establish that right-angled Artin groups containing a connected graph with more than one component satisfy this condition. We use this result to develop a novel method for creating subgroup systems and diverse intertribe distances in right-angled Artin groups. Specifically, for any positive integer k, we construct a collection of k pairwise independent subgroups within the right-angled Artin group associated with a fully transitive graph on 11 vertices. Our construction surpasses prior work on this subject.

In our proposed approach, we develop a novel non-parametric method using pairwise and long-range comparisons to effectively identify dynamic functional connections between time-series variables. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated across different data sets and under varying conditions, outperforming traditional state-based and comparison-based methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Our research findings are further supported by theoretical complexity analyses, indicating our method's optimal connection discovery performance and low computational cost. Implementations of our approach are made available for public use.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate a deeper understanding of phylogenetic networks, various methods for constructing and analyzing them have been developed in statistical genetics through mathematical techniques such as algebraic geometry and topological statistics. This study examines the underlying properties of three established methods for creating phylogenetic networks by comparing their reliability, efficiency, and sensitivity to different data sets, reticulate events, and user-defined parameters. The investigation shows that each method exhibits a distinct set of characteristics that affects its performance, and the choice of method should be made with consideration of the specific characteristics of the data and network in question.

Animal movement is key to understanding ecosystem dynamics, tracking disease spread, and monitoring environmental changes in ecosystems. However, analyzing large-scale video recordings of these areas is a labor-intensive process due to the high cost of human operators. Our system is designed to automate the identification of biological movement within video footage, particularly focusing on detecting moving objects below a threshold of 100 kg. By utilizing a deep learning-based approach combining U-Net and sort methods, our system reduces processing time and system costs, enabling real-time detection of biological movement in both compressed and uncompressed video.

The use of matrix inversion in optimization methods for solving multivariable problems has been well-documented. Advanced order techniques take advantage of a variable's limited range of change to minimize its impact on the objective function, thereby speeding up matrix inversion in subsequent iterations. We build upon earlier research by Gavrilovic and Hatanian, further refining their work to improve performance on GPU-based systems. Our enhanced framework maintains the efficiency gains associated with advanced order techniques while also facilitating a faster transition to subsequent matrix inversions, leveraging the computational capabilities of modern GPUs.

In scattering frameworks such as T-matrices and effective field theory for
scattering, a set of eigenchannels is identified that maximize energy absorption
at specific frequencies. This concept is applicable to any system that can be
described by a scattering matrix. Notably, the sum of energies within these
eigenchannels covers the total energy absorbed from the surrounding environment,
both within the system's inner regions and across its surface. Additionally, the
energy distribution within these eigenchannels can be analyzed through a series of
constraints that define the scattering matrix's properties.

Inspired by the Topological Anderson Model, we investigate topological properties in a three-dimensional Anderson model with randomly placed impurities in a binary configuration. Our study reveals that, depending on the average of the two uniform disorder potentials, the system transitions between distinct topological phases. Notably, we find that some topological phases emerge despite average disorder, whose boundaries we identify and distinguish between those resulting from localization and those from non-trivial symmetry breaking. Additionally, we find discrete mode crossings in self-dual points, confirming the requirement for topological phase transition in this model. Furthermore, we analyze the robustness of our findings through the evolution of topological invariants across the phase diagram.

This study focuses on a specific class of elliptic curves - those defined by equations in the form y^2 = Ax^3 + Bx^2 +Cx + D - and investigates two particular operations that can transform one curve into another within the same class. The first operation, known as trimming, involves modifying the defining equation by shifting the x and y coordinates according to certain formulas. The second operation, called isogeny, can map one curve to another more general form. Our research explores how both operations affect the underlying curves, with a particular emphasis on isogeny in voltage space.

Within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, the on-shell effective Lagrangian approach simplifies the complex renormalizable theory to a more manageable, two-loop Lagrangian involving the Higgs sector and its interactions with other fields. A key characteristic of this approach is the appearance of unwanted, quadratic divergences related to the Higgs naturalization process. In the present study, we tackle the challenge of systematically removing these unwanted divergences to ensure the Higgs parameters remain finite and physically meaningful. Our findings also reveal intriguing patterns of cancellation of the quadratic divergences, which stem from the intricate nature of the renormalizable theory. Ultimately, our research provides a clear framework for extracting the finite, physically relevant parameters of the on-shell effective Lagrangian directly from the infinite set of Lagrangian parameters, encompassing both the Higgs sector and the rest of the theory.

Conditional independence between features and historical values of a time series up to a specific point can be used to define linearity in network autoregressive models. Although this independence does not generally hold for all previous points, testing the condition using available data is still possible. In this study, we examine and evaluate linearity within network autoregressive models through newly introduced metrics that assess conditional independence. These evaluations enable us to explore and identify key factors affecting linearity, including model size, data length, and the type of network architecture. Findings show that network autoregressive models can achieve high linearity rates, exceeding 90%, when using relatively long data sets of up to 1000 points for analysis. However, linearity significantly declines when increasing the number of previous points considered for independence, from 3 out of 10 points having less than 90% linearity to almost all points falling below this threshold. Moreover, a interesting insight uncovered in this study is that, linearity generally increases with longer data sets, indicating there are beneficial connections between linearity and the natural fading memory property of NARX models.

In this study, we introduce a novel methodology using Issue-Frameworks for Factual Validation (If4FV) to assess the factual accuracy of neural network-generated text. We employ If4FV to investigate two areas of research: knowledge-based neural networks with focused question-answering tasks and realistic neural network-generated text. If4FV's effectiveness is demonstrated through two exploratory studies, and our approach is made available open-source for future research to build upon our findings.

A cell's behavior during dispersal is influenced by the movement of its cytoplasm, cell morphology and the activity of motor proteins that move along actin filaments.
This interconnection of biological processes at different scales makes live-cell imaging a challenging tool for studying cell dispersal dynamically.
To overcome these difficulties, we present a method for simulating cell dispersal in two dimensions, separating the system into three components:
a stochastic advection model for modeling fluid flow within the cell,
a state transition model for the movement of motor proteins on actin filaments,
and a geometric interaction model for the effects of cell morphology on motor protein activity.
We demonstrate the method's applicability to systems with varying levels of complexity, from a single actin filament to more complex cellular structures, and showcase its potential for generating simulations that mimic experimental data collection scenarios, including the impact of adding fluorescent dyes to the cell.

Our investigation uncovers the unseen force propelling users on Twitter to spread information about suspicious cryptocurrency transactions on the Ethereum blockchain, as reported on Etherscan, on the Ethereum Social (ethersocial) platform. Our analysis reveals the influence of transaction details, including sender and recipient information, on users' content creation. Notably, we found that users are driven by self-interest when referencing the sender's wallet, but their motivations become more complex when considering the recipient's wallet. Our findings indicate a desire for personal gain is stirred when referencing the recipient's wallet, but it is tempered by users' need to maintain a positive online image. This complex interplay is reflected in the varied language used by users to describe transactions involving well-known cryptocurrency figures. Our examination of the ethical implications of this behavior raises questions about users' willingness to engage with questionable content for personal benefit and how this impacts their understanding of cryptocurrency technology.

Large-scale quantum computing requires encoded qubits to withstand errors from the interaction between qubits and a noisy environment. In this context, we develop a coding framework based on reinforcement learning for fault-tolerant quantum computing. By viewing the encoding process as a series of single-qubit operations and quantum gate applications, we define a coding protocol that protects qubits from error caused by single-qubit rotations. Formulating the decoding process as a reward-based learning problem, we use reinforcement learning to develop codes that effectively minimize the error in the decoded qubit state. Building upon this foundation, we explore extensions to more complex quantum circuits, considering bounds on the number of stable qubits and encoding/decoding operations, and assess code performance with respect to error types and quantum circuit complexity. Our coding protocols, precluding the utilization of error correction codes like the surface code, offer promising code examples suitable for execution on devices like the superconducting quantum processor, enabling nearly error-free execution of critical quantum functions for cryptography.

Quantum metrology enhances measurement precision by leveraging the interplay between quantum fluctuations and the interconnection of entangled states. We've developed a method to achieve quantum win-win situations through the interaction of light in a double-cavity network. Starting from an initial entanglement of light states within two separate cavities, a semi-transparent mirror divides the light into two overlapping beams. As photon packets move towards each other, varying amounts of interference can be produced, allowing for the optimization of metrological measurements in both interferometric and single-ray applications. Using a double-cavity setup, we were able to achieve a significant improvement (the Heisenberg limit) in our estimation of a moving object's position, its velocity, and the optical distance, respectively. Estimating these parameters with minimal uncertainty required interacting photons for less than 10 times the optimal amount required without entanglement.

Researchers calculated direct photon-hadron correlations in Au+Au and d+Au collisions at 200 GeV to study jet interactions with the medium. Comparing results to p+p collisions allowed for an adjustment of systematic biases. After accounting for bias and flow-related effects, the analysis revealed a notable difference between Au+Au and p+p collisions. Specifically, the influence of flow on the distribution of hadrons relative to direct photons was more pronounced in Au+Au collisions. Furthermore, the presence of a medium-induced shift in the distribution of hadrons relative to direct photons was observed in Au+Au collisions but not in d+Au collisions, providing insight into jet-medium interactions in nuclear collisions.

This paper examines the universal Smarandache's sigma multiplication of digits $k \times n$ as $n$ reaches infinity, leading to a proof that for any positive integer $k$, there are infinitely many $n$ for which the number $10^n - 1$ is divisible by the resulting number. Furthermore, if $k$ is divisible only by the prime factor 2, it can be proven that there are infinitely many $n$ for which the resulting number is a divisor of $10^{2n} - 1$.

I'm excited to share our findings with the community, highlighting a critical yet under-explored factor affecting datacenter network design. The traditional hierarchical datacenter network architecture reduces congestion within individual tiers by limiting network access. However, the inherent variability of network allocation algorithms causes unpredictable behavior, threatening the performance and scalability of modern cloud applications. Through a comprehensive theoretical analysis and supporting experiments on real-world settings, our work reveals the inherent limitations of tiered networks in supporting high-concurrency workloads and showcases an innovative design solution that addresses this issue. By integrating semantic sub-networking into the OpenFlow framework, we successfully improve concurrency by tenfold and reduce overhead per packet by half. Our research offers valuable insights for cloud service providers aiming to optimize performance across various applications and workloads.

In our research, we're exploring a new model called the Situational Linear Bandit, which takes into account context and a unique response for each state. This model is used to manage systems that adapts to changing environments over time. We've developed an efficient algorithm for multiple agents to learn from their individual local observations without needing to share their data. When there are many agents, this algorithm reduces the number of updates required by a significant margin. Additionally, we've established that our algorithm achieves the lowest known regret rate for this type of learning. This achievement is particularly notable because it improves upon a method where all agents share their data jointly. We've also created a variant of an efficient algorithm for a specific scenario where the response is the same regardless of the context. This variant achieves a regret rate that's almost as good as the best known method for a non-situation linear bandit, but with a significant improvement in scalability.

This study explores the impact of remote working on the success of Scrum projects. To achieve this goal, a comprehensive survey was conducted among software industry professionals, resulting in valuable insights being gathered from 149 participants. A statistical analysis known as COIVAR was employed to examine the relationships between working remotely, team cohesion, and project outcomes. Furthermore, 27 participants consented to an in-depth interview, allowing for a more nuanced examination of the findings. The research revealed that remote working has both positive and negative effects on Scrum projects. On the one hand, working remotely was associated with improved communication approaches, increased flexibility, and a greater sense of trust among team members. On the other hand, it was linked to decreased face-to-face interaction, a higher risk of distraction, and difficulty in maintaining a work-life balance. Interestingly, the research indicated that remote working enabled teams to focus more intently on project goals, thereby reducing the influence of external pressures. We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by significant research on learning from biased data, particularly Chapter 3 of Citron and Mub basi (2019). We agree with Kallus (2020) that results in Theorem 2.1 and 2.2 are indeed extensions of results in Neyman and Rubin (1970) and Rubin (1973) to machine learning models. Our results related to Theorem 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 are however novel as they address balancing estimates based on biased samples for the values of interest not specified by the propensity score. We also extend results in Cai et al. (2017), Athneey et al. (2020), and Athey and Imbens (2016) to a broader class of machine learning models. We appreciate the reference provided by Kallus (2020) to Jia et al. (2020) which addresses balancing estimates based on biased samples for the values of interest specified by the propensity score, using a different approach than ours.

This study utilizes ALICE data from Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV to examine how elliptic flow is generated and influence charge particle distributions. An advanced analysis method is introduced to accurately separate the effects of flow and the initial condition through a parameter known as $\chi^2$. With an advanced event shape engineering method, $\chi^2$ values are adjusted to isolate elliptic flow influence on particle distributions. Results reveal strong $m_T$ dependence of elliptic flow, an observed trend in previous studies, and a lesser understood $p_T$ dependence. Additionally, elliptic flow is found to differ between light and heavy particles with increasing $m_T$, demonstrating how the quark and gluon composition of particles affects their movement.

Recently, the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform (QLCST) has been proposed, extending the Linear Canonical Transform, which itself is a broad generalization of the Fourier Transform. This new transform falls under the category of linear canonical transforms defined by a 2x2 matrix with complex entries. In this study, we investigate the ambiguity theorems for the QLCST. Firstly, we establish the conditions under which a linear canonical transform becomes its own inverse, a property that indicates periodicity in the frequency domain. These conditions yield two distinct sets of matrices with complex eigenvalues, which in turn give rise to two specific forms of the 2x2 matrix that define linear canonical transforms with periodic properties. Furthermore, we prove and demonstrate through specific examples that only transforms represented by these two specific forms will exhibit periodic properties in both time and frequency domains. These theorems provide valuable insights into the broader linear canonical transform family, extending beyond the QLCST to other transforms within this category.

This work extends our previous finding from a binary power binary interference network that the extremal sum generalization degree of freedom for K user networks can be $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$.  We enhance our previous result by demonstrating that the same $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ extremal sum generalization degree of freedom enhancement is achievable when power regulation is optimal.  We derive a lower bound for the K user case, and develop an upper bound with an extremely large, yet finite, number of users in the scope of a generalized version of a previously constructed code.  Our analysis yields the exact generalization degree of freedom for a duple interference network.  The answer to whether optimal power can be substituted with binary power in a triple interference network remains unanswered.

When simulating complex fluid-particle flows using integrated particle-fluid simulations, our new method allows for longer time step differences between the fluid and particle simulations without resorting to artificial particle movements. This method enables a more accurate representation of real-world particle interactions that extend far beyond the typical time frames captured in our simulations. Despite involving highly detailed particle collisions, our method still enables computationally efficient simulations by limiting the number of steps needed to model these interactions. This approach has significant implications for how we model fluid flow around particles, particularly in scenarios where multiple particles interact with each other and the surrounding fluid. Our research demonstrates that using this method, we can generate more realistic simulations of how particles behave in fluid flow scenarios with multiple particle interactions.
This article presents $3$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the fact that the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ has exactly whole number solutions for $a, b, n$ where $n$ is greater than $1$.

Our research focuses on a robotic monopod that performs lateral leaps on soft ground, incorporating a novel approach to simulate highly deformable environments through electrostatic sensors and realistic surface interactions, which ultimately facilitates enhanced feedback for its motion control system using a novel hybrid method combining feedforward and estimated terrain properties.

Hybrid quark models, combining linear confining potential and Coulomb force, effectively describe the properties of hadrons. In a previous study, spin symmetry was identified within the $s$-wave meson sector, allowing for the classification of mesons based on angular momentum properties rather than spin. This current research further develops that model by introducing a new concept, spin-singlet meson elasticity, which enables the description of mesons with higher angular momentum (l > 0) using the same principles as spin-singlet mesons. By applying this idea to mesons with elastic shapes, such as mesons composed of two or more quarks, it becomes possible to account for their internal structure and elasticity effects on physical properties. A key development in this research involves an expression for the elastic shape factor, which can be applied to any meson, regardless of quark composition or angular momentum. Using this expression, elasticity effects on mass spectra and radial wave function behavior are examined for several examples, showing significant impact in some cases. This research provides a foundation for extending the hybrid quark model to describe other composite systems.

A droplet in the presence of a surrounding gas, where there are varying electric field strengths, exhibits a complex behavior of oscillation that is captured by an analytical resonance phenomenon. This resonance occurs when the droplet's natural frequency aligns with the electric field's frequency, causing a pattern of oscillation called a "hydraulic fan". This study aims to provide an initial framework for understanding how droplet movements are affected by an external electric field, a phenomenon observed in spray aerosols.

Effective reasoning about complex text requires more sophisticated models that can grasp the meaning of subtle language cues, including negation.  However, the limited scope of existing datasets hinders the development of these models.  To address this challenge, we introduce CONDAQA, a novel negation-inclusive multiple-choice LAMDA comprehension dataset.  Featuring 8360 question-answer pairs on topics like science, history, and literature, CONDAQA is one of the largest and most challenging datasets of its kind.  Our evaluation shows that popular LAMDA models struggle to perform well on the CONDAQA dataset, especially when confronted with negated statements.  To improve performance, we propose a novel negation-aware training strategy for contrastive pretraining, which significantly enhances the accuracy of these models on CONDAQA.

This research proposes an innovative method for creating hierarchical structures in information systems. Our approach introduces 'hierarchy descriptions' as a new module in S-BACI, an established framework. Hierarchy descriptions serve as a bridge between information system representations and established methods for comparing objects. By integrating this component, we can now determine the most detailed information necessary to differentiate between distinct categories of objects within a given level of a hierarchical structure. In contrast to other approaches, our method can accommodate an unlimited number of attributes across each level of the hierarchy.

Quantum annealing shows considerable promise in addressing NP-hard optimization challenges, but the performance of this method can be hampered by imperfect quantum simulators, which often result in the loss of precise control over the annealing schedule. In response, researchers have investigated the consequences of deviating from optimal, precisely controlled quantum annealing protocols. This work investigates the dynamics of quantum systems during both controlled and uncontrolled freeze, quench, and annealing processes, with a focus on the precise cover problem. Our study reveals that certain uncontrolled scenarios can yield superior outcomes equivalent to those achieved through controlled quantum annealing, with implications for the efficiency of quantum annealing protocols. Furthermore, we identify distinct quench and annealing phases in this problem, highlighting the irreversibility of quantum annealing dynamics.

Business processes are frequently complex and intricate, yet their basic specifications can be quite limited, focusing mainly on individual process actions. To better capture processes, the concept of partial traces has been proposed, allowing for more comprehensive modeling. This approach can be further enhanced by considering prefixes and suffixes of process traces. Our research builds upon existing alignment techniques used to compare process executions against expected patterns, specifically for prefixes, suffixes, and mid-sections of traces. We also present an extension to handle cyclic behaviors within process executions. Additionally, we present solutions for determining whether a process execution conforms to a partial trace, either by finding alignments or using reachability analysis. This work can be applied to whole traces, including cyclic behaviors, and is demonstrated through examples using the BPEL language.

Using a dual-band model, we investigated the electronic properties of infinite-layer nickelate in its superconducting state. Nickel has the electronic structure of a Mott insulator with correlated $3d^8$ electrons, and substituting oxygen with $A$-site alkaline earth or rare earth hydrides creates a strong attractive interaction that drives this system into superconductivity. By examining the effects of electron pairing on the nickel's $3d$ orbitals, we found that the dual-band model results in highly anisotropic and $c$-axis-dominated $d$-wave superconductivity. Our findings also indicate that normal-state charge-dense regions are associated with electron pairing in the form of alternative patterns. These patterns prevent direct electron transfer, explaining the anisotropy of gap sizes. Additionally, we discovered that strong hybridization between the $4s$ and $3d$ orbitals is crucial for obtaining the dual-band structure. Further, we found that strong pseudogap states can be created by increasing the distance between nickel and the $A$-site ion through lattice expansion, which can provide a theoretical basis for studying the doped limit through comparison with the better-studied infinite-layer hafnium oxide system.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of initial data with low magnitude in the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation on an infinite domain. We demonstrate that solutions with a specific symmetry pattern, involving time-dependent temperature and concentration differences, exhibit distinct grazing behavior at opposite boundary limits along a specific trajectory. A novel diffusion phenomenon and a phase blending effect in the solutions are found to arise from the interplay between collisions and advection. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for the recent microlocal approach to studying the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation on an infinite domain.

We utilize radiance data from space to reevaluate wave characteristics over the ocean. By utilizing narrow spectral bands, we separate solar reflectance from aerosol and other contaminants. This allows us to apply the Cox-Munk and Marzano methods independently of in-situ measurements. Our approach yields previously unattainable global maps of wave characteristics, which show good agreement with wind speed measurements. Our findings also indicate that wave characteristics can be used to improve the estimation of solar radiance over the ocean.

The growing complexity of software systems necessitates a more efficient approach to detecting defects through reduced test scenarios. Our research into the parallelization of software systems test scenario reduction algorithm utilizing singular value decomposition has yielded promising results, which we will be detailing in this paper. We will outline the difficulties associated with decomposing the Centroid matrix found in the software systems' clustering phase and present an alternative method to achieve parallelization. A comprehensive test scenario reduction algorithm for software systems has been developed through further refinement of the decomposed matrices and application of the RANdomized Search (RANS) method. Our experimental findings have shown that this approach can successfully parallelize software systems test scenario selection.

The spread of the new coronavirus has had a significant impact on the worldwide emotion state, which can be reflected through microblogging contents especially on popular platforms like Hudong and Weibo. To better understand public opinion during the COVID-19 outbreak, this study focuses on classifying Hudong and Weibo user emotions using machine learning techniques. A comprehensive dataset consisting of Hudong and Weibo text was created for each of the four phases leading up to and during the Lunar New Year celebrations in 2020. Evaluation results showed that, when compared to baseline models, a random forest classifier performed notably better at predicting the emotions associated with Hudong and Weibo contents, achieving high accuracy rates of 84.5% and 77.5% respectively. Furthermore, our research revealed that text feature extraction using a word2vec model, specifically the word embedding method, yielded the highest performance metrics among all tested methods. Additionally, our findings indicated that there was a noticeable shift in public emotions during the four phases examined in this study.

In cuprate superconductors with an excess of electrons, there's a theoretical gap that could be bridged if certain interlayer conduction models are applicable. Largely based on data from "tunneling" experiments, these models suggest that an unusually large electrical current can flow between copper layers through a specific resonance caused by an unusual electronic state. However, these models have limitations as they don't account for other key experiments and don't provide a clear explanation of how this resonance is triggered. Our research aims to overcome these limitations by integrating elements from both the cuprate and strontium-calcium-copper oxide material groups. By doing so, we've developed a comprehensive theoretical framework that explains how interlayer conduction can occur through a non-resonant mechanism, leveraging a concept called electron-hole pairs that forms an oscillating charge density between copper layers. This new approach is supported by numerical simulations and offers a more flexible framework that can be applied to a broader range of situations, potentially leading to a more unified theoretical understanding of these materials.

The speed of sound in dense stellar matter is an essential aspect for the study of relativistic stars, especially when dealing with relativistic gravitational waves generated by compact object mergers or quark star collapses. Recently, Lattimer and Prakash found the adiabatic index to be greater than 4/3 when considering dense matter without strangeness at low densities, but below 4/3 at higher densities. Our research extends this finding to dense matter with strangeness by using a polytropic equation of state under both static and dynamic conditions, and we demonstrate that the adiabatic index can drop below 4/3 in high-density regions of quark stars. Our study also explores how different maximum neutron star masses are indicated by various sound speed patterns.

Counter tai mappings were originally introduced in relation to tai mappings, a set of transformations that changes arborizations into each other, preserving their associated permutations. We are expanding on this concept by creating a new set of transformations that further expands the already established relationships between arborizations and permutations. Specifically, we are demonstrating that applying a counter tai mapping to an arborization is equivalent to applying a tai mapping to the complement of its associated permutation. This newfound insight enables us to generalize the existing connections between arborizations and permutations, resulting in a more comprehensive understanding of these discrete structures. Furthermore, we are able to generalize the already established limitations on tai mappings, ensuring that they remain precise and accurate.

Constructing a bosonic Fock space using a compressed and translated coordinate basis, we derive a novel set of operators representing the canonical quantized position, momentum, and Hamiltonian. These operators maintain standard forms, despite the basis transformation. Further, we determine the conditions under which the compressed and translated basis retains the standard properties of the Fock space. Specifically, we find that only a specific rotation around the $y$-axis, composed of a 45-degree clockwise rotation and a translation in the $x$-direction, preserves the standard properties. This finding has implications for the development of a semi-classical simulation method for quantum many-body systems.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) may occur in protoplanetary disk systems beyond 0.1 AU from the sun. It is triggered by slow rotation in the outer disk and can cause the formation of ring patterns and structures. This study examines the effect of growing dust particles on VSI in the outer disk. It utilizes a combination of computer modeling and analytical techniques to investigate the stability of a protoplanetary disk system consisting of gas and dust particles. The findings suggest that as dust particles continue to form, VSI becomes less stable, ultimately disappearing when the mass of dust particles reaches a certain threshold. This effect is attributed to the increasing vertical shear caused by dust particles' accumulation in the midplane of the protoplanetary disk system.

We have established a new Liouville theorem for compact, subset-based Riemannian manifolds with constant scalar curvature and diminishing Ricci tensor. Building upon this finding, we have derived explicit formulas for constant scalar curvature, quasi-Einstein manifolds with diminishing Ricci tensor, expanding upon earlier work by the second author that focused on conformally flat manifolds.

Sequential neural network models often employ dynamic mechanisms in their initial stages to adapt to input sequences of unequal length. We extend this concept to any layer within the network by proposing Dynamic Entrance Modules, a portable and flexible mechanism that allows multiple entry points within the sequence-based network. Additionally, we integrate Global Mean Pooling to combine local features and facilitate the dynamic learning of sequence representations. This approach is then applied to Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks through a Dynamic Entrance Bidirectional RNN framework, resulting in a model that adapts its input processing based on input sequence characteristics. Experimentally, our method achieves superior performance compared to static networks and alternative dynamic approaches on multiple dataset benchmarks, notably improving accuracy on various sequence classification tasks by an average of 6.5% on the SemEval 2017 Task 1 and 8.8% on the STreeC benchmark, with further potential applications and results available on request.

High-accuracy astrometry provided by space-based missions like Gaia is subject to a influence that has long been disregarded: an imprecision originating from the deviation of general relativity's rules described by Post-Newtonian parameters. Through the variation of one specific Post-Newtonian parameter, $\gamma$, the measurement of parallax can be distorted by a amount equal to $\gamma$ times 10^-8 multiplied by the square of the ratio between the position of an object and its distance to the centre of the Milky Way. Given the maximum possible impact of this effect on parallax measurements, it's evident that $\gamma$ needs to be determined with a precision better than 0.001 by future missions that determine parallaxes accurately.

A groundbreaking new approach has been introduced that uses cutting-edge machine learning tools to rapidly simplify complex dynamic systems. By leveraging observations of a system in flux, a reduced version can be created that accurately predicts future behavior across various scenarios. What sets this method apart is its incredible speed, needing only minimal computational resources and a mere fraction of time compared to traditional techniques. This approach has been shown to yield remarkable results for intricate systems involving multiple interacting variables and different types of physical phenomena.

In model systems featuring high-frequency modulations of potential, our analysis through both analytical and numerical methods reveals that initially localized waves in one-dimensional, multi-component Bose-Einstein condensates exhibit enhanced stability. This increased stability allows for the reduction of required initial conditions, enabling the creation of persistent, localized excitations even in the presence of group velocity mismatch between components. Our findings also indicate that this self-amplifying effect can lead to the formation of stable breathers through a weak modulation of the inter-atomic interaction, facilitating a transition from a soliton to a dimerized state.

This research proposes a breakthrough method to safeguard machine learning model confidentiality in scenarios where input data and model are shared with an untrusted entity. The proposed solution, SIMC 2.0, builds upon previous work by introducing an adaptable linear solver that addresses performance concerns and develops an efficient protocol for model updates in anticipation of future attacks. Key advancements include: optimizing computation for machine learning through floating point operations; designing a secure multi-party protocol for linear equations with dynamic participant roles; and a protocol for upsampling numerical data without compromising performance. Notably, our research reduces the average computational overhead associated with the secure training of machine learning models by nearly an order of magnitude.

Using the FAST radio telescope, we have significantly expanded our knowledge of the M101 galaxy group's HI structure. Our data shows that the system contains numerous HI clouds beyond its member galaxies, as well as a newly discovered HI tail extending over 110 kpc behind M101. This tail is likely a consequence of interaction between M101 and its nearby galaxy, NGC 5477. Additionally, we have found additional HI clouds at radii of approximately 150-300 kpc from M101's center, at velocities that align with the galaxy's HI envelope. These clouds may originate from a nearby galaxy group known as the M101 group's southern substructure, which was previously detected using the GBT.

To effectively answer questions based on common sense, it is not enough to simply rely on broad, general knowledge about language. A new approach, called Coarse-to-Careful, generates a preliminary answer based on a coarse-grained semantic search, refining it later with more care. This method aims to address one key limitation of existing approaches - the lack of semantic connection between questions and answers. By integrating a neural network designed for semantic matching, the approach generates responses that exhibit a semantic connection to the question at hand. When put to the test on the CommonsenseQA benchmark, our method proves to be a more efficient and accurate way of answering questions, outperforming leading baselines in both metrics.

A crucial aspect of astrophysics research is identifying and understanding the underlying processes responsible for molecular spectra, particularly in environments with high temperatures and energetic conditions. To accurately interpret satellite data and simulate the composition of molecular gases in various environments, a comprehensive knowledge of molecular spectra is essential. Although significant progress has been made, there are still substantial knowledge deficiencies in the spectra of certain oxygen-containing molecular cations, which are prominent in cometary atmospheres. This study sheds light on the need for further spectral characterizations of oxygen-containing molecular cations, based on a comprehensive analysis of cometary spectra using a set of high-resolution spectra from the Hubble Space Telescope. By analyzing the (1-0) S band of CO+, the study found that existing characterizations are sufficient, whereas the (v=1-0) band of HCO+ and HCO+ in its ground vibration state require further study. A theoretical approach was also used to estimate the absorption cross-sections of these species under conditions similar to those found in a comet, and the results showed that while CO+ can be detected through its (1-0) S band even at a distance of several million kilometers from a comet, HCO+ may not be as easily detected through the (1-0) S band of HCO+.

We investigate how to effectively break down a quadratic form into a sum of squared values in a global domain, particularly within the realm of number fields. Our research broadens a significant finding by Minkowski, relating to the number of perfect squares available in a given range of values. Our findings also provide a useful technique for studying the number of elements with specific properties that can be generated through a combination of quadratic forms.

We're proposing a new method using photonic technology to efficiently match celestial object spectra. This approach simplifies the process by eliminating the need for time-consuming and computationally demanding comparisons with vast astronomical database collections. Instead, our system leverages advanced algorithms to perfectly match the patterns of object spectra with those of reference sources through optimal rotations of photonic frequency axes, effectively circumventing challenges related to temporal and radial velocity shifts. Furthermore, our system is highly adaptable, enabling seamless incorporation of new spectral patterns via updated photonic frequency rotations, thus facilitating seamless and efficient object source identification, even in complex scenarios.

Relational deep learning in medication pair evaluation addresses the challenge of identifying potential adverse interactions between prescribed medications. Our investigation aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of this field by examining various models using medication pair datasets, such as TargretInhib and MMTD. Our research involves implementing multiple relational model architectures using the Learning to Rank (L2R) and Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks, training and evaluating them on existing datasets using additional features and a score-based sampling strategy. Our findings demonstrate that through careful feature engineering, certain GNN-based models can match and even surpass the performance of existing models without the need for data augmentation techniques. Furthermore, our study highlights several key observations, including the importance of preprocessing techniques in graph-based models and the potential limitations of existing datasets in the field.

The classic Itô-Wentzell theorem significantly broadens the applicability of change of variables formula in stochastic analysis, enabling the integration of functionals of stochastic processes through a change of variables. Our research builds upon this foundation by extending the theorem to path spaces with uneven norms, enabling a change of variables formula for a wide range of functionals of stochastic processes with varying time parameters. The specific settings considered include the stochastic differential equation, the Brownian motion with random parameters, and the semi-martingale with random parameters. These extensions significantly broaden the scope of the Itô-Wentzell theorem, demonstrating its profound impact on the analysis of stochastic systems through a change of variables.

Federated learning enables multiple entities to collaborate on training a shared model. A significant challenge in FL is dealing with diverse data distributions across participating clients. We propose a novel random walk method to tackle this issue. In traditional machine learning, models are optimized to perform well on the training data. Conversely, our 'Stroll for Education' approach advocates for a more exploratory strategy, where the model's objective is to visit as many regions of the data space as possible. This is achieved by adapting the model to minimize a custom penalty function that assesses the frequency of visiting specific data points. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields compelling results for reducing the data distribution disparity and improving the model's performance on previously unseen data when compared to conventional federated learning methods.

Numerical simulations of rotating fluid flows using the anelastic approximate equations have confirmed the previously theorized spectrum of decaying rotating turbulence for high rotation rates. These simulations modeled a freely decaying flow in a triply periodic box with a strong rotation constraint. Analysis of the simulated data showed that it aligns with the theoretical spectrum of cascading energy found in 1995 by Cambon, Scotti and Genshall, as well as a specific kinetic energy distribution discovered in 2004 by Cassou-Estruch and Cambon. However, predicting the spectrum of simulated wave turbulence remains a challenge due to contamination from nonlinear interactions distorting the energy distribution according to the simulation resolution. A specific kinetic energy spectrum was identified in the simulated data when accounting for the resolution-dependent distortion, and it revealed a distinct inertial wave chaos regime with a specific triadic structure. This regime exhibits a unique and resilient spectrum of cascading energy that differs from the conventional Kolmogorov-Zakharov spectrum.

Individuals within the criminal justice system exhibit elevated levels of distress and poor mental well-being. Research indicates that compulsory therapy is capable of yielding positive outcomes for this population; however, further investigation is required into the specific benefits it affords in terms of psychological well-being. This study assesses the effects of compulsory therapy on mental health in an incarcerated sample comprising both male and female participants. Results revealed that compulsory therapy led to substantial improvements in psychological well-being for both genders, with outcomes persisting post-release from prison. Additionally, analysis uncovered that compulsory therapy induced notable reductions in self-harm tendencies in female participants. These findings hold implications for the integration of compulsory therapy into the criminal justice system's mental health interventions within incarcerated individuals within this vulnerable population.

Specially designed models can accurately label specific parts of an image,  but when it comes to filling in unknown areas,  existing methods typically rely on general regularization techniques  to prevent overfitting.  A fundamental issue with current approaches is that they often ignore the basic requirement of having a consistent solution when applying transformations to input data.  To address this limitation,  we propose a novel regularization method that incorporates a consistency constraint  based on the fundamental principle of invariance,  effectively enhancing the performance of healthcare image segmentation tasks  especially in scenarios with limited labeled data.  Our technique demonstrates superior results  compared to leading semi-supervised image segmentation methods  on commonly used benchmarks and has the added benefit of  being extremely lightweight.

To handle increased data rates in future experiments like the ATLAS detector for LHC's High-Luminosity era, the jet calorimeter trigger system requires a significant upgrade to process events at a 300 Hz rate. This project involves integrating an advanced, custom-designed board based on an Ultrascale+ FPGA into the system to achieve this goal. The board, developed with the support of IBM researchers, incorporates several innovative features to efficiently process events. It utilizes a novel multi-FEMB (Field-Embedded Memory Board) architecture to enhance memory access and a high-speed, bidirectional data path to optimize data transfer between the FPGA and memory. The board also employs a cutting-edge, 7-series interface to efficiently transfer data to the host system. To test its performance, a prototype of this board was integrated into the ATLAS jet calorimeter trigger system and subjected to a 700 TeV proton-proton collision environment replicating the conditions expected in the LHC's High-Luminosity era. Results show that the board meets the system's requirements and can process events at a 300 Hz rate.

Our novel approach uses a unique neural network to generate highly detailed, 
customizable virtual human avatars in real-time. Unlike traditional 3D 
modeling methods that rely on rigid meshes, our system uses an innovative 
articulated framework consisting of interconnected skin segments, inspired by 
human anatomy. Each segment is mapped to a specific mesh component, such as 
a knee joint or an eye. This design allows us to leverage the benefits of 
both articulated models and neural networks. During training, our system uses a 
self-supervised technique that combines automatic rendering of avatars and 
real-world photos, ultimately mastering the creation of highly realistic, 
customizable virtual humans. Our system's unique features include the ability 
to generate low-poly avatars at high speeds and more complex, detailed 
characters in real-time. Moreover, it offers seamless texture integration and 
emulates light and shadow effects, further enhancing realism.

We propose a novel neural network approach using a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to track the dynamics of quantum systems, specifically for the hydrogen molecule in this case. Our GNN-based model excels at predicting local electron behavior and providing insight into quantum chaos through the consistency of predictions, essentially serving as a bridge between quantum chaos theory and quantum computing. By leveraging explainable artificial intelligence techniques, we break down the chaos of quantum interactions into clear predictions, illustrating how our model accurately assesses quantum chaos by analyzing the reliability of predictions in stable and chaotic electron states.

In statistical inference, combining data from different groups to estimate a common parameter is highly beneficial, and this combination is called parametric averaging. Our study focuses on assessing the average parameter of a mixture of independent observations using maximum likelihood estimation, and we develop an estimation method that addresses issues related to boundary parameters and misspecification. We investigate the asymptotic properties of our proposed estimator and show that it achieves the same efficiency as the traditional maximum likelihood estimator under proper conditions. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for the variance of the estimated average parameter when the individual components' variances are known. Our work also addresses the challenge of estimating the variance of the average parameter when the parameters of the mixture components lie within specified ranges. We propose a transformation method to transform the boundary parameters into finite values, and this approach has implications for sampling problems. Our results can be applied to settings with equal or unequal proportions of mixture components.

Knowledge tracing has emerged as a technique to monitor and adapt to changing student knowledge based on performance data from interactive learning tools. Recent research combines knowledge tracing with machine learning models that learn from student interaction data, offering more precise predictions of subject matter mastery. Although the field has made rapid progress, evaluating and comparing the effectiveness of these methods remains a challenging issue. A lack of standardized evaluation protocols and diverse benchmark datasets for knowledge tracing and related tasks hinders researcher understanding of what machine learning features work well on the associated data types. To address this gap, we've developed pyKT, an open source evaluation framework for testing deep learning based knowledge tracing systems. This tool provides features for handling diverse dataset formats, preparing training and test data for evaluation tasks, and conducting comparisons between different models. By utilizing pyKT, researchers can focus on exploring new machine learning methods for evaluating and comparing knowledge tracing models.

Let's consider a smooth projective variety $X$ of higher dimension and a smooth divisor $D$ within it, with no overlap in their singular points. If we have a smooth manifold $X'$ that extends $D$, we can determine if there's a global section for a specific type of elliptic operator on $X'$ by analyzing the same type of operator on $X$.

We've designed Alethe to be a versatile proof format that can be used in various SMT solvers and proof systems. Alethe builds upon the CVC3 and Yosysfolio proof formats to create a more comprehensive and adaptable language. To achieve this, we've extended the language to better incorporate formulas, functions, and proofs. This extension allows us to express a wide range of formulas, including those with bitwise operations, length functions, and more. Furthermore, our proof format can represent multiple proof types, such as saturation-based proofs, induction-based proofs, and more. To validate Alethe, we've converted several SMT solvers to generate Alethe proofs and successfully used these proofs to test multiple SMT solvers that support Alethe proofs. Our results show that Alethe can support a wide range of formulas and proof types, making it a useful tool for the SMT community.

As models become more dependent on private data for protection, secure federated learning becomes more practical. Optimizing models in a secure and efficient manner is crucial for successful deployment. Current secure federated learning techniques face challenges in balancing efficiency and optimization effectiveness due to data heterogeneity and limited communication. This paper introduces a novel aggregation method called buffered synchronous aggregation, allowing for greater model optimization without significantly increasing communication costs. During communication, participating devices send the mean of their optimized gradients, capping at zero, thereby addressing issues with heterogeneous data and negative gradient clipping. This method is mathematically proven to maintain convergence with relaxed communication constraints. Experimentation with real-world datasets demonstrates improved model accuracy using the proposed method.

Recent studies on transfer learning for end-to-end ASR have achieved significant improvements, enabling near-top-finish performance on native languages without native data, using non-native resources. Our research explores two key aspects in this field: detailed-to-detailed and coarse-to-detailed transfer. In a monolingual setting, we found that transferring from a rough transcript to a detailed transcript is more challenging than transferring from one transcript type to the same type. To address this issue, we proposed two main approaches: one that incorporates a phoneme-level alignment model to enhance transfer learning from a rough transcript, and another using a mask-based decoder to adapt a cross-language ASR system from a rough transcript in the target language to a detailed transcript in the source language. Our experiments showed that both approaches can achieve substantial gains, with the phoneme-level alignment model delivering particularly promising results.

Graphs are utilized in numerous applications due to their capacity to model connections and hierarchies among entities. Nonetheless, complex networks pose difficulties for both structural role-based node embeddings and proximity-preserving node embeddings methods. To address these challenges, a new dataset named Twitch Players has been introduced, based on data from the Twitch streamer network. Evaluations of various node embedding techniques including node2vec, roleguiding, DeepWalk, and TASTY have been conducted to assess the accuracy of classifying streamers into different categories according to their gaming specialties. The results indicate that node2vec outperforms other methods and facilitate the creation of visually appealing illustrations of the Twitch network. Furthermore, applications of the Twitch Players dataset have demonstrated its versatility and openness to collaboration and further research possibilities.

To clarify the nature of $K\bar K$ resonance $f_X(1500)$, we performed a comprehensive reanalysis of existing data from $B\to \pi K$, $B\to KKK$ and $B^0_{(s)}\to \eta K^0_S$ decays using an R-use approach, considering both magnetic dipole transition and electroweak transition. Our primary findings indicate that $f_X(1500)$ can be distinguished as a $K\bar K$ resonance at around $1500$ MeV, with uncertainty margins of $20$ MeV in mass and $100$ MeV in width. Notably, our results demonstrate that this resonance can be identified with the $K\bar K$ component of $\rho^0(1450)$. Systematic and statistical uncertainty margins of $K\bar K$ mass and width of $\rho^0(1450)$ are found to be $[1441,1461]$ MeV for mass and $[1095,1315]$ MeV for width. Our analysis further reveals that $\rho^0(1450)$ contributes around $55\%$ to $B^0_{(s)}\to \eta K^0_S$ decay rate. Moreover, we derived upper bounds for $\rho^0(1450)$ to $K\bar K$* and $\phi(1600)$ decays, which could be

We present a theoretical model proposing that approximately 37% of Dark Matter consists of Primordial Black Holes. To support this idea, we develop a multi-dimensional concept comprising four distinct areas: the Observable Dimension, the Hidden Dimension, the Marshland, and the Esoteric Dimension. The Hidden Dimension is analogous to a "marsh" - where all information about the Observable Dimension becomes distorted due to the high gravitational effects in this realm. The interaction between the Hidden and Observable Dimensions defines the "marshland," resulting in the distortion of light being emitted from the Observable Dimension, which we perceive as Dark Matter in the Hidden Dimension. The Esoteric Dimension represents a 'true' void within this multi-dimensional structure. Our model proposes that Primordial Black Holes inhabit the Marshland Dimension, distorting space-time in a way that makes them invisible to us. The distortion also explains the phenomenon of Dark Energy observed in the Observable Dimension. The remaining 63% of Dark Matter, according to our model, resides in the Esoteric Dimension. The four dimensions in our theory have unique properties, which we outline in detail. The model also predicts that Primordial Black Holes will eventually be detectable when the distortion of space-time becomes significant enough to allow their presence to be ascertained.

A key challenge in controlling series elastic actuators lies in the significant distortion of the elastic material's measurement readings due to forces unrelated to the intended movement, necessitating an accurate estimation of the actuator's true force. A novel force estimation algorithm is introduced, utilizing a transmission force observer that takes into consideration the elastic actuator's characteristics and calculates the desired force for smooth movement. However, implementing this algorithm proves complicated due to the unobservable nature of the desired force. A novel approach involves modifying the force observer with the desired force derived from a simplified kinematics model, successfully enabling the estimation of the actual force. Computational testing of this algorithm was conducted using MATLAB Simulink, demonstrating reliable and precise force estimation in various scenarios.

A raft made of a brittle material that's subjected to tension will inevitably crack, and this damage propagates in various possible ways. This research aims to examine how a raft's fracture pattern is influenced by the location and size of inclusions within it. It's known that inclusions can significantly impact the stress distribution within the raft, creating areas of high tension that could potentially dictate the path of crack development. By running numerous simulations with varying inclusion positions and sizes, this study creates a comprehensive map of possible fracture patterns that result from different stress distributions. This map of fractures provides valuable insights that could also be applied to other types of structures that feature inclusions, such as pavement systems.

We analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate multiple interacting scalar fields with varying symmetries, specifically including both SO(Nf) chiral and unitary symmetries. By exploring the phase plots and determining the conditions for stable Higgs phases, our findings reveal that Higgs phase regions exist for both symmetry cases when the scalar potential exceeds a certain threshold, albeit the conditions differ. The requirements include a positively curved potential and a critical mass threshold that varies with the number of fermion flavors. The results demonstrate a distinct distinction in the phase plots conferred by the unitary and chiral symmetries of the SO(Nf) group.

To enhance marine robot navigation using sensory data, our novel approach introduces a new method for extracting relevant time-based pattern information from sensor signals. By combining Gaussian Process regression with a sparsity-promoting prior, our algorithm efficiently discovers and models significant changes in signal variations over time. The proposed method is easy to implement, computationally straightforward, and effectively captures important temporal variation features in comparison to more complex methods. Our results demonstrate that incorporating the algorithm into marine robot navigation using sensory data leads to superior performance.

This paper introduces a novel sorting network called the "Maximal Sorting Array" (MSA), which interestingly features the fewest number of comparators among all known uniform-depth sorting networks, achieving this low depth of $n-2$ while handling inputs of length $n$. Our analysis demonstrates that the MSA's comparator structure, comprised of a sequence of nested folded sorters,  efficiently detects any out-of-place elements within the input array. Furthermore, we discovered that employing multiple instances of the MSA in a hybrid approach leads to sorting arrays with even smaller depths, specifically $n-\sqrt{n}-3$, which represents the most minimal uniform-depth sorting networks encountered to date.

We establish a novel, non-uniform two-fluid model for rotating stars consisting of distinct fluids, developing a comprehensive relativistic stellar structure framework. By comparing our model to existing approaches within both General Relativity and Post-Newtonian theory, we clarify its key benefits and limitations. Furthermore, our research offers innovative solutions to complex astrophysical problems, including pinpointing neutron star compositions based on their mass and spin, as well as developing novel methods to identify rotating neutron stars using gravitational waves emitted during a companion star's death in the companion star's preferred emission band.

Using semi-analytical models and numerical simulations, we study how a spiral galaxy's starry arms are formed. We ran multiple simulations in a highly baryon-rich universes, creating 10 high-resolution $N$-body models of a Milky~Way-like galaxy. In each model, a spiral galaxy forms and develops structure over 1 billion years. We examined the pattern of star formation in these galaxies through analyzing their far-infrared and UV emissions. Our findings show that in a baryon-rich universe, a spiral galaxy's star formation follows an exponential distribution along its spiral arms. We also found that in a baryon-rich universe, gas clouds collapse more quickly in areas with higher gravitational potential, resulting in more massive galaxy bulges. Additionally, we found that a spiral galaxy's supermassive black hole's mass is directly proportional to the galaxy's bulge mass. We ran additional simulations to investigate the role of a galaxy's central black hole in its bulge's formation, but found no significant impact.

We investigate how strong magnetic fields affect galaxy interactions, considering both gas and stellar components, in a three-dimensional cosmological simulation. Our analysis shows that a significant influence of magnetic fields is necessary to prevent the disruption of both gas and stellar disks during galaxy collisions. When magnetic fields are weak, the increased turbulence and jet formation have a minimal impact, largely due to the overwhelming effects of shock waves. In contrast, strong magnetic fields successfully restrict the flow of gas and stars, preventing their disks from being distorted. Interestingly, we found that in galaxy interactions, the influence of magnetic fields on gas and stellar components behaves similarly, with the effect being greatest in regions with moderate to strong field strengths.

Our solution proposes a cutting-edge machine learning technique for accurately identifying COVID-19 cases based on chest images, incorporating advanced data processing methods to enhance performance. Our approach utilizes a sophisticated classification algorithm called the infection-aware contrastive mixup classification model, successfully achieving superior results on the CDC COVID-19 Detection Challenge by significantly reducing error rate and outshining existing competition.

Most current research focusing on grammatical error rectification has concentrated on standard supervised learning models, utilizing vast amounts of labeled data to train them. Nonetheless, labeling datasets for grammatical errors is extremely time-consuming, especially in new domains, where resources might be ample but labeled data is scarce. Consequently, developing methods that can quickly adapt to new domains without needing extensive labeling becomes essential. In this paper, we propose leveraging meta-learning to achieve such domain adaptation. We introduce a meta-facilitated agent that learns from experience in multiple practice domains and subsequently transfers that knowledge to new target domains with limited labeling. Results indicate that this approach yields highly competitive performance on previously unseen domains, notably outperforming the baseline model trained on a single target domain by a margin of 10.14% in F1 score. Furthermore, our model's ability to adapt across domains with substantially reduced labeling requirements is critically examined, revealing a notable reduction of 24.53% in needed labels.

Rounding on surveys can lead to inaccuracies in research estimates when respondents round their individual values to the nearest integer. Previous studies suggested that people tend to round to the nearest higher or lower number based on the total number of options, but these findings have been disputed. This study examines how people round their individual values when they know the total will be an exact sum of the respondents' answers. Under these conditions, the rounding strategy appears to be unrelated to the number of options. Instead, the data suggests that people round their answers based on the total number of options multiplied by a specific factor, effectively dividing the range into equal segments. This disputed result holds significant implications for research using data from surveys rounded to the nearest integer.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of GdInO3, a material that only exists in a highly oxygen-deficient state. They studied its structure, found to be centered on a honeycomb lattice, and found a very low value for the magnetic exchange interaction constant in this direction. Using various techniques, they found that magnetic ordering occurs at a very low temperature and characterized its structure. Additionally, they observed a unique shift in some peaks in the infrared spectrum. Furthermore, we found that magnetic ordering can be explained by a mean-field approach, and calculated the strength of the magnetic exchange interaction in the honeycomb lattice.

The problem of allocating essential resources among self-interested agents, where the agents' actions can affect the allocation, is an important issue in economics, mathematics, and computer science. By utilizing game theory and combinatorial optimization, we develop a method for finding suitable and fair equilibrium allocations by ensuring that any proposed allocation can be part of a pure Nash equilibrium. This approach allows us to create allocations that are both efficient and fair, meeting specific requirements based on various fairness criteria such as fairness, equity, and more. Additionally, our approach provides an optimal solution to the equity problem, which has not been achievable with previous methods. To further advance the field, we also introduce the concept of strong fair strong Nash equilibria and prove that it is combinatorially NP-complete to find solutions to the equity problem using strong fair strong Nash equilibria.

When adapting to a new domain in an unsupervised setting for transfer learning, most current methods overlook the possibility of having multiple possible scenarios. Unlike these approaches, our proposed framework is more adaptable as it can handle various situations that may arise when adjusting to a new domain. Instead of focusing solely on ideal cases, our model is designed to recognize both domain-specific patterns and the differences between them. When applying this to image classification using the Domain Adaptation Protocol, our results show that our proposed model outperforms the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin. Moreover, our model's code and model are publicly available for download.

A rare and unique star-forming region has been discovered in the spiral galaxy UGC 8839, located in the Ursa Major constellation. A comprehensive study of UGC 8839, conducted using radio wave observations, reveals a large and distinctive non-rotating disk in this galaxy. This massive disk, measuring approximately 48 kpc in diameter, shows extremely low star formation activity levels. In contrast, the surrounding areas of UGC 8839 exhibit typical levels of star formation. The unusual characteristics of this large disk in UGC 8839 cannot be adequately explained by existing models of gas dynamics using numerical simulations. Further research is necessary to better understand the unique features of this massive disk in UGC 8839.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an innovative type of detector, to study dark matter. These detectors have the ability to analyze track formations left behind by high-energy cosmic rays that interact with dark matter. Unlike traditional approaches, paleo-detectors don't rely on particle collisions or signal counts, but rather examine geometric patterns resulting from the interactions. This method allows paleo-detectors to detect dark matter at much lower energy levels, beneath the sensitivity threshold of current detectors. As a result, paleo-detectors have the capability to conduct more sensitive dark matter searches and provide distinct signals that can be verified through independent approaches, enhancing the validity of their findings. Furthermore, paleo-detectors offer the opportunity to search for dark matter across various time periods by re-analyzing existing rock formation samples from different geological ages, offering a flexible detection approach.

This paper presents DP-Sync, a novel framework that addresses the problem of protecting update trends in cloud-based databases by leveraging differential privacy. The issue with encrypting and outsourcing database updates is that an untrusted cloud server can deduce sensitive information about the user's activities based on update frequencies and patterns. Our approach transforms frequency-counting queries into private synthetic workloads that conceal update trends, enabling efficient and secure execution of common database operations while ensuring the protection of sensitive activity data. Through performance evaluations using real-world datasets, we demonstrate that DP-Sync achieves comparable efficiency to non-private synthesis methods. Furthermore, DP-Sync ensures protection against numerous potential attacks, including those that exploit update trends.
