Specifically, our proposed architecture, comprising six layers of a residual fractional batch normalization unit within a residual framework, has been successfully utilized in a dataset that was randomly partitioned into training and testing sets. Notably, the incorporation of this architecture into our experiment led to the accurate identification of outlier images, which were subsequently manually re-examined to validate the efficacy of this method. Further research will explore integrating this feature with class imbalance techniques.

Researchers study a variant of the Hele-Shaw cell featuring a rotating disk, where an less dense liquid is attempted to be displaced by a more dense liquid. The introduction of a surface imperfection causes the more dense liquid to invade the less dense liquid in a curved pattern. Due to the cell's confined nature, the influence of surface tension cannot be ignored. As the rotation speed increases, the influence of surface tension diminishes, revealing a broader symmetry associated with the Kuramoto-Sinai-Yorke algorithm. A theoretical model is developed to explain how surface tension distorts the pattern of invasion in a variety of conditions.

In this work, we introduce an innovative approach that bypasses the constraint of preserving phase space volume, commonly seen in standard Hamiltonian dynamics methods, including the generation of Hamiltonian trajectories, the construction of Hamiltonian boundary conditions, and Hamiltonian constrained equations of motion. We demonstrate that our method specifically circumvents the inherent volume alteration associated with the phase space, achieving a precise correspondence with standard Hamiltonian dynamics through the utilization of Hamiltonian pathways, especially in the case of an unconstrained expansion.

Recent studies on ethynyl derivatives of aromatic molecules have led to a discovery of a new isomeric form, ethynyl cyclopentadiene, within the TMC-1 cloud complex by utilizing the GALACTIC center HII region spectral synthesis and fitting program and radiative transfer calculations. This finding was confirmed through both general (CMAME) and detailed (LEGA) chemical models, which predicted the presence of two cyclopentadiene isomers, namely ethynyl cyclopentadiene and benzene, within the cloud. A comparison of column density results showed that ethynyl cyclopentadiene has approximately one-fifth the amount of benzene's column density. Moreover, an assessment of the CCH to CN ratio in ethynyl cyclopentadiene revealed a value significantly lower than in c-C_H and benzene, which may indicate a greater impact of isomerization in the interstellar medium on the formation of cumulene molecules or a more efficient destruction pathway of the CCH form through reactions with atomic hydrogen.

In generative neural network-based text generation tasks, attention mechanisms are commonly used to control the production of additional descriptive text. This research introduces an innovative 'look-ahead focus' approach to address this challenge. By leveraging a self-update strategy to assess future content, our model is able to prevent the inclusion of irrelevant information in the additional text. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in two applications: (1) enhancing sentence descriptions with explicit linguistic labels, and (2) generating more precise text summaries in structured document formats. Our model's performance is compared to a representative baseline model, and we find that it significantly outperforms the baseline in both evaluation metrics.

The introduction of new technologies is often met with skepticism in established fields, but we believe that translating the concepts of service-oriented architecture into the terminology and practices of database research holds significant potential for enhancing current approaches and methods. By redefining traditional notions of services, data, and applications through a SOA lens, we can refine methods for designing, testing, and optimizing databases. Our efforts in translating these concepts into the language of database research culminated in a SOA-inspired framework for designing data management services, which in turn influenced the development of grid databases and services. Our experience demonstrates that importing innovative technologies into established fields requires a flexible and adaptable mindset, willing to integrate novel ideas into existing knowledge and practices.

We've developed a new cosmological model that incorporates a dark substance with decay and formation rates, forming a complex system driven by conservation principles. This model is based on a simple equation that describes the evolution of the universe, and through mathematical analysis, we've identified a precise solution that represents a significant improvement over the conventional $\Lambda$CDM model. Our analysis utilizes numerical methods to simulate the universe's early stages, and our findings show that our model can generate intricate cosmic patterns without the need for initial fluctuations. By applying our model to observational data from supernovae, cosmic microwave background, and galaxy statistics, we've found a good fit without requiring any adjustments, and our model outperforms the $\Lambda$CDM model according to the Akaike information criterion and Bayesian evidence. Our model predicts a constant Hubble rate in proportion to the speed of light, and we've verified this prediction through direct Hubble constant measurements. Our model also forecasts future Hubble constant measurements above a certain threshold of accuracy, offering a means to test it through observation.

In educational settings, curiosity is a vital skill that curiosity-driven learners need to develop, and it's essential to measure their curiosity dynamically throughout the learning process. This study proposes a novel, multi-faceted approach to measure curiosity in educational interactive digital content using physiological and visual interactions of learners. Our research team developed a theoretical framework suggesting that curiosity varies over time and is influenced by prior knowledge, motivation, and learning goals in learners. To test this framework, we designed an exploratory study for small groups of learners in interactive science lessons. Our data analysis revealed the curiosity of learners fluctuated throughout the study and was shaped by their initial understanding of the subject, their motivation to learn, and their interest in the content. Notably, we found that middle-school students exhibited higher curiosity levels compared to high-school students in our data. Our findings highlight the potential of using physiological and visual data to gain a deeper insight into the curiosity levels of learners in group settings. Additionally, we suggest that our approach can be applied to assess the effectiveness of educational content in fostering curiosity in learners.

In statistics and machine learning, Gaussian processes are renowned for their versatility in predicting unknown function outputs given corresponding input values. A key characteristic of Gaussian processes is their square-exponential kernel, which facilitates efficient prediction computations. Notably, this kernel can be reinterpreted as a property of graphs, where the likelihood of observing data at specific graph nodes influences the predicted function values at those nodes. This perspective enables the derivation of alternative kernels, such as the Mat\'ern family, by analyzing the properties of graph functions and their respective smoothness levels. Our results demonstrate that traditional Gaussian processes can be viewed through this graphical lens and provide a framework for constructing novel kernels with distinct characteristics, such as changes in smoothness level or exponential decay, among others.

Metropolitan mobile sensing with ridesharing vehicles offers immense potential in monitoring urban infrastructure, yet their optimal deployment strategy remains an unresolved issue. A previously proposed method for detecting road defects relied on vehicle location data, but its limitations in accuracy and scalability necessitate a more effective approach. This paper converges mobile sensing with network theory to design an optimal detection method for monitoring road systems, addressing issues like vehicle sampling, route selection, and data utilization. Our model utilizes graph theory to model road systems and mobile sensing, and develops an algorithm to determine the minimum number of vehicles required to detect all roads within a system. This minimum number serves as a measure of the method's scalability and efficiency. To evaluate our method's efficacy, we conducted numerical analyses and simulations based on real-world data from New York City and Chicago. Our results show that a small fraction of vehicles can be optimal for detection, and that our method's performance improves with increased vehicle counts, paving the way for practical implementation of metropolitan mobile sensing with ridesharing vehicles.

A deviation in the decay width of the J/psi meson into a single photon and an invisible pair could indicate a need for new physics beyond the Standard Model. A dimensionless quantity, R, is used to represent the difference in the decay width as a fraction of its total. In a recent LHCb experiment, R was found to be within the expected range of 0.5 to 0.6, although a value of R greater than 1 would be necessary to significantly explain the within 1 sigma variation of the neutrino minimum within the context of the electroweak symmetry breaking theory. A value of R greater than 1.3 would be necessary to explain the minimum within the context of the seesaw mechanism. A LHCb experiment is expected to provide a value for R with a certain level of precision by the year 2025. If R is found to be within a certain range, it could provide evidence for new physics within the range of a few TeV and offer a means to investigate the properties of new physics through variations of R in future lepton and dark energy experiments.

Second-order differential equation-based dynamical systems can be solved using an established method that involves explicit and implicit integration. A previously developed algorithm for this case applies a fixed timestep in an explicit first step, followed by an implicit second step using a formula with a weighted average of the Euler and Runge-Kutta methods. This paper explores the potential for variable timesteps starting with an expanded A-stable implicit formula that uses four function evaluations. Properties of this new method were investigated and it shows comparable performance to the original fixed-timestep algorithm.

This study introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) for analyzing multivariate functional time series data, integrating the benefits of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA) and functional singular spectrum analysis (FSSA). By adapting the SS-AF approach for analysis along one, multiple, and all dimensions, MFSSA offers enhanced forecasting performance, as evidenced by results from simulated and real-world data experiments. The code and a demonstration are freely accessible on GitHub. Furthermore, a user-friendly R-package named'mfsa' has been developed for easy implementation of the methodology.

Our analysis reveals that models utilizing the Advanced Encryption from Neural Network-Based Quantum Computing (ANEQ) encryption scheme demonstrate both excessive reliance on training stability and heightened sensitivity to training parameters. This complex behavior is attributed to multiple interconnecting factors, including difficult optimization, inadequate secure classification, insufficient utilization of encrypted data, and the inherent flaws in the neural network encryption method. In order to enhance the security provided by NEQ-based classification models, it is essential to address and mitigate these underlying issues.

This study examines the time a particle spends within a set distance from its initial position as it moves according to a stochastic differential equation with decreasing drift. To be precise, we determine the probability that the particle's distance from the starting point exceeds a certain threshold for some duration below a given time frame. Our analysis applies to a specific type of stochastic process where the drift term varies inversely with the square of the displacement and is influenced by an external force. The problem can also be solved for cases where the drift term has a linear relationship with the displacement and for certain conditions involving exponential functions.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is undergoing a transformation to accommodate new diagnostic tools and a helicon-based plasma source. A comparison between the original plasma source and the new helicon source has been carried out using a range of diagnostic methods, including laser fluorescence, charge exchange, and Langmuir probes. The measurements show that the helicon source achieves similar plasma conditions, with some differences in plasma structure and particle fluxes. Notably, the helicon source produces a more uniform plasma in the direction perpendicular to the magnetic field, whereas the original source exhibits a clearer distinction between the central plasma core and the edge plasma. The particle flux measured by Langmuir probes is significantly higher in the helicon source, but the reasons for these variations are not yet fully understood. The study confirms that the new helicon source can effectively replicate the plasma conditions necessary for relevant ICRF experiments.

In biological control systems that utilize competitive exclusion to suppress invasive plant species, a model is developed to analyze the impact of a microbial pesticide. The model is a system of ordinary and partial differential equations that simulates the interaction between beneficial microorganisms, target pathogens, and weeds in multiple spatial locations. It is demonstrated that, without considering spatial variation, the model's equilibrium points can be analyzed through a Hopf bifurcation, ultimately leading to the extinction of both pathogens in a completely dominated scenario. When spatial variation is accounted for, a Hopf bifurcation occurs at a critical threshold, resulting in periodic oscillations that lead to the coexistence of beneficial microorganisms and target pathogens in a quasi-periodic regime. It is also shown that a spatial wave train emerges at the bifurcation point, characterized by alternating stable and unstable patterns. This discovery provides insight into the complex dynamics of a microbial pesticide system and highlights the critical role of system stability in achieving a desired outcome of complete pathogen elimination.

In precision medicine, accurate cancer cell nucleus detection is crucial for further diagnosis and treatment planning. Currently, a major obstacle hindering automated detection is the limited availability of annotated training data. We introduce a novel approach called W-Net, a dual-stage network that combines a feature-extraction module with a region-proposal module, allowing for nucleus segmentation from unannotated images and the proposal of accurate regions for annotation. W-Net outperforms state-of-the-art competitive models on multiple evaluation metrics, achieving superior results on both annotated and unannotated images with minimal additional training.

Let's consider a number field $k$ and a Galois extension $k$ to $K$, with a Galois group $G$ containing a subgroup $G_0$ that isomorphic to $A_{p-1}$ or $D_{p-1}$ and acts on a group $V$ over $K$. Additionally, let $V$ be a free $K$-module with a specific dimension, and let $\rho$ be a $G_0$-homomorphism from $G_0$ to the group of $K$-rational points of $V$. This paper explores the possibility of extending $\rho$ to a homomorphism from $G$ to the group of $K$-rational points of $V$. We provide conditions under which such an extension is feasible, given that $G$ acts on $V$ in a specific way and can be broken down into a product of subgroups with similar structures. These conditions ensure that the initial component, defined by its action on $V$, does not contribute to any non-trivial fixed fields of $K$. We further establish that if $G_0$ is isomorphic to $A_{p-1}$, the necessary condition can be restated in terms of the structure of $V$. Moreover, we demonstrate that if $G_0$ is isomorphic to $D_{p-1}$, a similar condition applies when $V$ has a specific

A graph G is considered detectable n times if its n-th iterated line graph, denoted as G^n, contains a Hamiltonian path. The concept of detectable graphs is an analogue to the properties of traceable graphs that contain a Hamiltonian path when an edge of G is removed. This paper delves into examining the characteristics of graphs that are detectable n times, including investigating how many edges need to be removed from G for its n-th line graph to have a Hamiltonian path.

Cell death through pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation and large cell lysis, can be triggered by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death similar to apoptosis, yet distinct in its mechanisms and consequences. The scope of our project is to develop a single cell population model that captures the key mechanisms leading to SARS-CoV-2 induced pyroptosis, as well as the impact of anti-inflammatory treatments on the host cells. Specifically, our model incorporates NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1 autolytic processing, IL-1 beta secretion, and the subsequent NLRP3 recycles that lead to a cascade of pyroptotic cell deaths. Building on previous research, our model extends the NLRP3 recycle model proposed by Huang et al. [1] by incorporating the role of anti-inflammatory drugs, such as statins, in modifying the basic reproduction number (Rt) and ultimately affecting the pyroptotic cell death rate. A key finding of our project is that the model reveals several key parameters that influence the basic reproduction number (Rt) and pyroptotic cell death rate, including how anti-inflammatory treatments can decrease (Rt) and slow down pyroptotic cell death. Furthermore, our model demonstrates that increasing key parameters like the recycling rate of NLRP3, the processing rate of caspase-1, and the secretion rate of

External observations about state variables not directly influencing the goal of an agent are often ignored in reinforcement learning research. However, such information can sometimes aid the agent in achieving its goal by providing additional context. In scenarios where this information is unavailable, the agent's performance may suffer. To address this, a new framework is introduced that seeks out and utilizes external state variables for enhanced goal attainment. To prevent overreliance on external information, a goal-oriented agent must also be incentivized to explore and discover all relevant state variables. Two protocols are devised to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, resulting in goal attainment with reduced episode counts and a distinct agent behavior characterized by sustained curiosity. The proposed framework is asset-free and universally applicable, as demonstrated through a diverse range of state space scenarios.

A blockchain-based smart contract on the Tezos network offers Michieli et al.'s compiler a fully formal specification through a type of refinement type. Our project HELMHOLTZ is a refinement type-based validator for these contracts, allowing for efficient and automated verification of their behavior on the Tezos network. During this process, refinement types are converted into a more advanced format suitable for evaluation by the liquidhaskell tool, a proven technology for ensuring the correctness of Tezos smart contracts through liquid liquid applications. This combination of Michieli et al.'s compiler and our project results in a practical method for proving the correctness of these contracts before they are deployed on the Tezos network.

Recent studies have introduced new message passing techniques for graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) based on the fundamental concept of message passing, leading to improved performance in various applications, especially molecular property prediction. A new approach has been proposed, using matched filtering, to break down the GCNN filter function into individual message passing steps, providing a clear mathematical understanding and making it possible to analyze the filter function through a factorization approach. This new perspective offers a more in-depth exploration of the GCNN filter function and its relationship with the Boltzmann machine, enabling the exploration of new message passing techniques that match mathematical rigor. This approach is a significant step towards a more unified understanding of message passing in GCNNs and may facilitate the identification of efficient and effective message passing algorithms that can enhance performance in molecular property prediction and other applications.

By formulating Einstein gravity in a 3-dimensional spacetime as a Chern-Simons theory for the gauge group $SO(1,2)$, we can express the Einstein-Hilbert action as a Chern-Simons action for the gauge group $CS[so(1,2)]$. This formulation allows us to incorporate a scalar field and redefine the Chern-Simons action to obtain a new 3-dimensional gravity action linked to a scalar field. This redefinition results in a gravity action that comprises both Einstein gravity and a scalar field action, enabling us to depict spinning hairy black holes and solitons within this framework, even when gauge fields are present.

We've observed that Sp(2)$\mathbb{R}$ symplectic metriplectic systems possess a non-reversible counterpart, characterized by the reversal $\tau$ that flips the sign of the symplectic form. This paper explores a specific instance of this phenomenon within branes for Sp(2)$\mathbb{R}$ Poisson manifolds. Our study reveals that branes for non-degenerate leaf spaces are equivalent to those for the corresponding symplectic algebras, whereas branes for degenerate leaf spaces are connected to those of the non-reversible counterpart under the $\tau$ transformation. This connection provides valuable insights into the classification of the non-reversible counterpart through the branes of the reversible system.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the visualization of tissue pathologies by displaying the physical properties of tissues. It combines the strain imaging of tissues with their mechanical characteristics, achieved through the injection of a contrast agent or mechanical stimulation. Ultrasound elastography offers a non-invasive means of visualizing tissue mechanics. However, the precise calculation of tissue mechanics is hindered by the limitations of ultrasound technology, particularly its inability to accurately measure lateral distances. This research proposes a virtual origin synthetic aperture (VOSA) method to enhance the estimation of lateral displacements in ultrasound elastography. The VOSA method utilizes the synthetic aperture ultrasound technology in conjunction with the virtual origin concept to improve the spatial resolution and estimate lateral displacements with greater precision. The performance of this method was evaluated through numerical modeling and comparisons with existing techniques, and it showed significant advancements in estimating axial and lateral displacements. The results indicated a notable increase in the correlation coefficient from 0.83 to 0.94 for the axial direction and from 0.57 to 0.92 for the lateral direction. The research outcomes suggest the potential of the VOSA method to enhance the precision of ultrasound elastography.

Students learn programming best through practical experience with a specific language, but to facilitate learning, a general scheme of pseudocode is commonly used. However, traditional pseudocode is often designed with clarity for human readers in mind, rather than students new to programming concepts. To bridge this gap, we introduce a variant of pseudocode that uses logical deductions to guide students through problem-solving processes, even if they don't fully grasp the underlying code. When executed, this code generates a more student-friendly version with explicit error checks, ultimately producing a working program in a language like Python. Through this approach, students can explore and modify the code even if they don't fully understand the original pseudocode, using their problem-solving skills to overcome errors along the way.

We examine how the Boolean function $f_v$ behaves in relation to posets of a V-shape, specifically those of length three or more, within Boolean structures of varying depth. Our analysis determines the degree of the function $f_v$ to be $\frac{3^{n+1}-3}{2}$ when working with posets of length three, and $3^{n+1}-3$ (or $2^{n+1}-2$ when restricting to linear orders) for posets of length four or more. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which $f_v$ is maximised at $1^{\binom{n}{2}}$, and determine its optimal value at $\big(\frac{3^n - 1}{2}, \frac{3^n + 1}{2}\big)$. Additionally, we explore Ramsey properties associated with $f_v$, including the behaviour of $f_v$ in linear orders and its connection to the Ramsey property of complete V-shapes.

In our research paper, we examine the performance of the dynamic $k$-means clustering algorithm in identifying groups of similar data points. Our analysis applies to data sets with a high number of features and a moderate number of data points. We demonstrated that a modified version of the algorithm, which forms clusters based on the minimum distance to a specific neighbor, achieves nearly optimal results in both theory and practice. This improvement benefits from the use of a specific metric that gauges the algorithm's efficiency, which in turn relies on an inexact bound derived from an existing study on the minimum distance to the $k$th nearest neighbor. We also explored the limitations of the traditional $k$-means algorithm through a dimensionality reduction technique known as PCA, showing that it may fail to detect certain clusters even when the data points are well-separated.

We introduce hierarchicalcombinatorial policies in Stochastic Pursuit-Withdrawal Games, which unify previous approaches by leveraging both combinatorial and hierarchical structures. Our key contribution demonstrates that hierarchical policies yield significantly better performance in evaluated scenarios, outperforming non-hierarchical methods by several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we facilitate solution scalability through reduced action spaces, achieving computationally efficient solutions with significant gains in application domains like transportation systems.

A key requirement for likelihoods to compare alternative models is circularity and the absence of transitive property. Unfortunately, finding counterexamples proved challenging for over fifty years. Our discovery offers an important advancement in likelihood theory. We demonstrate how counterexamples can be found, thereby addressing a significant obstacle in the theory. Our findings also reveal that circular likelihoods are necessary for model selection. We examine the conditions under which likelihood ratios exhibit the nontransitive property and propose a new classification system that distinguishes between strong and weak circularity. Ultimately, we establish that likelihood ratios must be strong to facilitate effective use in model selection.

Recently, deep learning methods have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, mainly because they can balance noise preservation and image quality improvement in noisy medical images. A key technique in this area is the unsupervised cycleGAN, which allows training networks using noise-free high-dose CT images as fake data. However, the performance of these networks is limited by their inability to process dose extremes far from training data, such as very low-dose CT images. To address this issue, we introduce a new AdaIN-switchable cycleGAN framework that enables the generation of CT images across a wide dose range. The innovative aspect of our approach is the incorporation of a dose-aware module into the unsymmetrically connected discriminator, which facilitates the extraction of image features related to the CT density. By leveraging this extracted information, the network can effectively switch between training and testing phases, producing realistic fake high-dose images and enhancing low-dose images without relying on paired data. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior quantitative evaluations and visually pleasing restored images, outperforming state-of-the-art cycleGAN networks in terms of PSNR and SSIM.

Recent advances in dialog comprehension pre-training have primarily built upon contrastive learning pre-trained models like BERT and Mask-RNN. These pre-trained models are typically fine-tuned for specific tasks using limited labeled data. We introduce SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for dialog comprehension tasks. It extends semi-supervised contrasting pre-training using a pre-trained model for named entity recognition and generates contrastive dialogs through a loop mechanism. The model is trained on vast amounts of unlabeled dialog data and leverages a minimal amount of labeled data for NER tasks. We evaluate SPACE-2 on the SICK Dialon and OOS dialog datasets, achieving notable improvements over existing approaches. Notably, it achieves a significant 11.5% boost in OOS accuracy and 1.8% boost in SICK Dialon's main test set when using a NLU evaluation metric.

We've established a local isometry between an ideal fluid spacetime's conformal Ricci-Yamabe manifold and a particular type of soliton, specifically a conformal (k-{\theta}-flat) soliton, where k and {\theta} have specific relationship. Additionally, we've defined key concepts within the context of an ideal fluid spacetime. We've demonstrated that an ideal fluid spacetime's conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton exhibits (k, {\theta})-flatness, a property that can be used to analyze its invariant vector fields and the fluid's potential non-degenerate nature. Furthermore, we've identified conditions under which an ideal fluid spacetime's conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton can be a gradient soliton, a condition related to the fluid's non-degenerate nature.

To study the distorted structure of p-shell halos, we used the angular momentum projection method on $^{16}$C, $^{20}$C, $^{24}$O, and $^{24}$Mg. The DISTAL potential successfully simulated the exponential decay of these nuclei' density outside their central and symmetry zones. For low-spin states, the DISTAL potential accurately replicates the experimental data for magnetic dipole moments and binding energies with or without coupling. However, decoupling increases the predicted energies and dipole moments for higher-spin states, aligning with theoretical predictions following the rule of large numbers.

Video super-resolution involves restoring high-quality video from low-quality, pixelated footage.  This process is complicated by video's inherent properties of temporal noise, light and dark fluctuations, and repeated pattern duplication.  Existing super-resolution techniques are primarily designed for image enhancement and often overlook video-specific patterns.  By ignoring the temporal aspect, these methods can produce unnatural effects and slow down processing time.  Our proposed BasicVSR++ model addresses these limitations by incorporating a more precise motion analysis using optical flow and revised spatial and temporal fusion processes.  By combining motion analysis with initial predictions and incorporating contextual information, we significantly improve video super-resolution quality and efficiency.  Our model outperforms previous super-resolution models in still images and achieves state-of-the-art performance on video super-resolution according to PSNR metrics, while also surpassing the efficiency of image super-resolution techniques.

This work presents a novel approach in estimating vector boson momentum in muon-based experiments, specifically focusing on intrinsically uncertain muon tracks. Our method efficiently leverages existing measurement data, reducing the uncertainty by approximately half when compared to the conventional method. This improvement is particularly significant, achieving a greater reduction in uncertainty than expected from a simple scaling of the initial conditions. This approach has been applied to relevant muon interactions, demonstrating the ability to enhance precision in the subsequent estimation of form factors and other key physical parameters.

In complex reinforcement learning environments with multiple tasks, a key challenge arises when the learner encounters partial task failure during training. This difficulty prompts the introduction of a novel issue, the "catastrophic interference problem," which stems from an existing solution to multi-task reinforcement learning. To address this issue, the authors develop a new approach using modular separate learners for each task, a method they dub the "separate systems architecture." This architecture is then applied to two designs: a simple separate learner system and a more sophisticated design using shared representations. To train the latter, the authors create a third layer of modular coordinators that integrate the knowledge from individual agents through a coordinating mechanism. Empirical findings across various settings demonstrate that the proposed solutions effectively mitigate the catastrophic interference problem, reducing the degree of failure during training and facilitating learning in complex, multi-task environments.

This article provides an estimate for the error in approximating solutions to time-dependent porous medium type and swift diffusion type equations, specifically in a broad, noncompact metric measure space with a confined boundary.

We correct a common misconception regarding Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem in 1931. It has often been misinterpreted as stating the non-existence of a universal theory capable of proving all truths. However, we demonstrate that this misinterpretation originated from a linguistic error affecting the formula's translation. By rectifying this mistake, we establish that Godel's original proof already implied the existence of a single, universal theory encompassing all formal language within the scope of the given axiom system. Additionally, we explore the historical context surrounding this error and its influence on the development of ideas among Godel, Carnap, and others.

This paper formulates the three spheres theorem for functions solving the real, first-order, irreducible Dirac equation over complex Euclidean space. Specifically, we demonstrate that any non-zero, scalar function u defined on the Euclidean space \mathbb{R}^n, where n is 2 or greater, possesses the property that there exist precisely two spheres passing through the origin with the isolated common intersection point, at which the Dirac equation's solution u assumes a non-zero value. This theoretical advancement extends to the analysis of the associated Dirac operator's eigenfunctions in \mathbb{C}^{n+1}.

In the context of the Ising model with Glauber dynamics, where partially observable state transitions are present, the goal of Consecutive Spatially Equitable Sampling is to achieve a balanced representation of local configurations to facilitate efficient MCMC sampling. A previously developed method by Otsu and Goshima equates equivalence to the occurrence frequency of each configuration in a stationary distribution and proposes a criterion for equivalence that ensures a balanced representation. However, this approach has limitations in its applicability due to the uncomputability of frequency values. In contrast, a novel method is introduced that leverages the properties of harmonic functions in graph theory to provide a computationally feasible solution for determining equivalence, thereby expanding the scope of applicable models.

In tasks that require robot-assisted visual object localization and manipulation, instructing the robot to adjust its eye-in-hand camera is an essential step. Traditionally, this process involves providing multiple images, but our research aims to streamline this training by utilizing a single image. Our proposed method first employs a rotation augmentation technique to create additional views from a single training image, thereby reducing the number of training images needed. To further improve performance, we integrate a minimal set of training images to reduce the perceived ambiguities during the learning process. The benefits of our approach are validated through experiments using real-world datasets and a simulation environment, showing that our method excels in scenarios using a limited number of training images. Notably, in our experiments, our approach successfully learned from as few as one training image in some cases.

In applications like imaging and signal processing, an unknown input is recognized by how it transforms into an observable output. A key problem becomes identifying the input given the output and certain noise-prone measurements. A popular approach involves using a GAN-based algorithm to resolve this inverse problem by searching for an input that matches given output and measurements. Two significant issues arise with conventional training methods for such algorithms: the need to generate synthetic measurements during training and difficulty in controlling the quality of the generated samples. A novel conditioned generator is proposed to address these concerns by incorporating two regularization terms and a conditioning strategy. Two benefits result from this innovation: the avoidance of synthetic measurement generation during training and the incorporation of data quality control through a maximum likelihood estimation. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm facilitates efficient sampling by implementing a cost-reduced sampling method. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments in the fields of seismic imaging and magnetic resonance imaging.

This article examines the concept of locally invariant surfaces in the context of fractional-order dynamical systems. Unlike their integer-order counterparts, we demonstrate that fractional-order systems do not possess surfaces with this property outside of specific equilibrium points. This theoretical limitation applies to a broad class of surfaces, including those defined by polynomial functions. A notable example included in this study is the surface defined by $x^{\alpha} + y^{\beta} = 1$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are fractions within the range $(1, 2$.

THz wireless communications have tremendous potential to overcome the data transfer limitations imposed by the massive demand for data. Nevertheless, extremely short transmission distances and intense attenuation of THz waves impose significant challenges to system designers. To address these issues, a novel multi-hop architecture has been proposed to extend transmission distances and improve signal strength. This approach introduces new challenges related to optimal beam training, particularly considering the restricted data transfer capacity in each hop. To tackle this problem, a reinforcement learning method has been developed for each hop to determine the optimal scanning pattern, based on limited feedback information. The proposed scheme shows substantial gains in terms of training time compared to a baseline method, without compromising much on energy efficiency. Simulations validate the performance of the proposed approach in a realistic scenario.

The line-of-sight to a pulsar can provide valuable insights into the interstellar medium by analyzing the scintillation pattern of the pulsar's signal. By linking radio astronomy observations of the scintillation pattern with data from the MAXI X-ray telescope, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of how the distribution of electrons in the interstellar medium affects scintillation. Applying this approach to the bright pulsar B1133+16, scientists observed a scintillation pattern that changed over a relatively long period of 155 days, likely influenced by the movement of a large cloud of gas and dust within the Carina Nebula. This discovery may imply that similar formations exist in other nebulae and could have a more widespread presence.

This paper proposes a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, an
  pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network within the WaveNet framework.
  By incorporating a Lissajous curve-based feature extractor, a pitch detector,
  and a dilated convolution neural network, QPNet generates high-fidelity speech
  waveforms. Our model enhances WaveNet's speech synthesis capabilities by
  incorporating a dilated convolution neural network and provides a technical
  achievement in speech synthesis using an autoregressive raw waveform generative
  model.

This research presents the MADARi platform, an online tool developed to facilitate
the annotation of Arabic morphological structures and the correction of misspelled
Arabic words. MADARi builds upon the MADAR corpus, a comprehensive database of
morphologically analyzed Arabic words. Each entry in the corpus consists of the
standard Arabic script, transliterated Latin form, base word, part of speech,
number/gender, and a structural analysis known as the pattern. The MADAR corpus
contains over 43,000 unique words, making it an invaluable resource for various
NLP applications and tasks. However, the corpus's effectiveness is hampered by
inaccuracies in the analysis of a substantial number - over 30% - of the included
words. To address this issue, MADARi has been designed to enable a collaborative
effort among NLP experts, linguists, and native Arabic speakers to accurately
annotate and correct the spelling of Arabic words using a web-based interface.
The platform allows users to search for words by prefix matching and includes a
set of predefined part-of-speech options. A demonstration of the system's
spelling correction component is also included in this paper.

As exoplanets are increasingly found to orbit close to various types of low-mass stars, understanding how they interact with their host stars' light is becoming increasingly vital. A key aspect of this interaction is the chemical alteration of an atmosphere caused by photochemical reactions of molecules with the star's light. This study targets molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrogen, ammonia, and water vapor in atmospheres surrounding K and M stars. It involves a detailed analysis of how these molecules are affected by their absorption of the star's light and any resulting chemical reactions. The research uses a complex system of reactions and collisions to model these interactions and considers multiple possible atmospheric conditions, also exploring the potential for atmospheres to be influenced by their host star's mass exchange with its companion star in binary systems. The study finds significant differences in how molecules are affected by their absorption of light, with complex systems of reactions and collisions resulting in significant increases of up to ten million times in molecules absorbed by their atmospheric effects. It also discovers that highly reactive molecules such as nitrogen and oxygen are significantly affected by their collisional interactions, leading to large increases in their absorption of light. In contrast, less reactive molecules such as water vapor, carbon dioxide, and methane are primarily affected by their absorption of light. The study finds that atmospheres around K stars exhibit the highest levels of photochemical activity, with analysis of the spectral distribution revealing how to design future missions to detect the molecules in question. To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and other causes, we propose using tunneling spectroscopy with resistive electrodes that incorporate ohmic dissipation. Introducing a finite tunneling barrier height and applying a small voltage can help distinguish the gaps by adjusting the tunneling current in response to changes in bias voltage. While this method offers some advantages over previous techniques, implementing tunneling spectroscopy with ohmic dissipation through electrodes that incorporate contact resistance may also pose certain challenges.

The creation of a innovative system, named RoadAtlas, for the automated inspection of highway surfaces is presented in this research. This intelligent system uses drone technology and machine learning algorithms to analyze and classify highway defects in real-time. It offers a range of benefits, including reduced inspection costs, faster deployment of maintenance crews, and improved road safety through early identification of potential hazards. Additionally, RoadAtlas includes a user-friendly web platform that enables seamless data sharing and easy access to asset information.

We demonstrate that shadows, a concept recently introduced through the shadow coeffective functor, essentially serve as a bicategorical extension of the fundamental concept in classical algebra, specifically by drawing an analogy with linear systems that have a component of relative dimension one.

Locating sound sources is a fundamental aspect of human perception, integral to both visual and auditory senses. While visual localization literature is vast, there is a notable shortage of studies on auditory localization. Our research addresses this gap by extensively examining the identification of sound sources across various frequencies, environments, and head movements. Our findings reveal that high-frequency sound sources are consistently located more accurately than low-frequency sources. This precise location can vary depending on the frequency produced and is particularly precise at middle frequencies (around 2500 Hz). What's intriguing is that this optimal frequency for maximum accuracy may shift based on the surroundings and head movement. Interestingly, our data indicate that the most challenging sounds to localize are those with very low frequencies or high screeches.

Multi-layer graph neural network architectures are typically designed to be symmetric in both message passing and aggregation operations. However, this symmetry is compromised when distance-based functions are employed, such as those using the Lorentzian distance, to propagate node embeddings through a neural network. Our research introduces an asymmetric graph neural network model, where the forward and backward functions of message passing and aggregation have distinct forms. Specifically, we propose a Lorentzian graph neural network (LGNN) model that leverages the Lorentzian distance in forward propagation and employs cumulative activation to aggregate messages in reverse. LGNN exhibits superior performance in comparison to conventional GNNs, for which we provide theoretical justifications. Our model's efficacy is further demonstrated across diverse datasets and tasks, including node classification on SPAM, cancer treatment on TCGA, and link prediction on Citeseer.

The acoustic model we are using, which is based on a specific mathematical framework, cannot be directly seen from the data presented. However, with sufficient information, we can reverse-engineer the model by applying a specific method that utilizes Gaussian Process regression. Notably, this approach has successfully demonstrated the model's susceptibility to structural manipulation in the absence of noise, successfully recovering the original model. Furthermore, this approach has successfully recovered a model based on a structure that is a non-trivial modification of the original structure.

In a three-component system consisting of an optical cavity, an electrical resonator, and a mechanical oscillator, we examine the phenomenon of squeezing in the mechanical oscillator's stable state. Using a full quantum hydrodynamic approach, we find that a specific parametric matching can significantly increase the mechanical oscillator's squeezing amplitude by approximately 1400 times. Furthermore, we propose a diamond-based optomechanical experiment to test this phenomenon, taking into account losses associated with the diamond's phonon-phonon interactions.

We enhance the modal $\mu$-calculus with the ability to manage sets of objects, introducing both a propositional operator and a modal operator for doing so. By examining the relationship between this expanded language and a related propositional fragment, we are able to determine the complexity of basic operators within the expanded language. Furthermore, we establish that the propositional fragment itself becomes more complex, specifically entering the realm of PSPACE complexity for both its overall decision-making ability and that of its individual components.

This study introduces an exponential delay devaluation model inspired by
Tsallis statistics, a non-conventional approach developed to address
unpredictability in complex systems. Our proposed model builds upon existing
theories of choice function approaches, such as the Luce (1949, 1956) and
Anderson (1970) models, and extends them through a non-entropy Tsallis
quasi-arithmetic mean. In particular, we explore a specific instance based
on the harmonic mean, which provides a viable alternative to the standard
exponential model. This new model explores distributional properties and
synergy effects and could serve as a relevant framework for examining choice
behaviour data. We demonstrate the feasibility of estimating model parameters
using maximum likelihood estimation and conduct a limited analysis of the
estimated model.

We're exploring how gravity's strength is influenced at the harmonic function's core, specifically within the framework of $f(R)$ gravity models. By defining a specific harmonic function that reflects the deviation from standard General Relativity, we can apply its properties to extract relevant information about the gravitational field. This approach allows us to derive a specific expression for the Ricci polynomial $f(R)$ that's consistent with the boundary conditions imposed by the de Sitter universe, resulting in a specific solution for the Ricci scalar that indicates a shift from standard cosmological evolution due to the impact of the gravitational constant on the Hubble parameter. This discrepancy could be attributed to the heavy gravity phenomenon occurring when the harmonic function's minimum value switches from positive to negative.

A new class of graphs called expanded double covers (EDCs) is introduced, which is a superset of double covers. We establish that both basic and extended EDCs are limiting cases for specific families of graphs undergoing homomorphism preservation. Specifically, a graph G undergoes a homomorphism preservation transformation to become a basic/extended EDC if and only if it contains an induced subgraph isomorphic to a specific basic/extended member of the EDC class. This relationship is reflected in the use of the term "limit" for extended EDCs, mirroring the homomorphism preservation theorem. We further prove that both basic and extended EDCs have multiple equivalent definitions and demonstrate how they can be locally modified without altering their underlying structure. This involves showing that both basic and extended EDCs can be constructed through a process similar to R. Bouchet's method of constructing double covers through 1-2 toggles, although the name "toggle" would not apply.

Using Weyl-Wigner transforms, we relabel and reexamine the classical and quantum versions of the canonical distribution, ultimately illustrating their equivalents in phase space. This approach facilitates a comparison between the two distributions through a transformation of variables. Furthermore, our method enables a discussion of quantum corrections to its classical counterpart.

We discussed the concept of negative absolute temperature, emphasizing its
theoretical foundations, relevant models, and experimental verifications. Negative
absorption within resonant systems allows for the creation of stable, localized
traps for photons. This phenomenon arises from the complex nature of these systems,
which can be understood through the study of quantum field theory. The negative
temperature of these systems holds promise for increasing the efficiency of optical
communication technologies. Our review also explores potential applications in
quantum computing and the manipulation of atomic and molecular states.

Let G be an additive group of integers, and S a nonempty subset of G. We investigate the quantity A^+_k(S), defined as the maximum value of the sum of k conjugate positive elements, where the sum is taken over all possible combinations of elements from S, subject to the constraint that the sum of the elements' absolute values does not exceed |G|, divided by (k*|G|). Our main objective is to determine lower and upper bounds for A^+_k(S), with particular interest when k is greater than or equal to 2, and our methods also yield new inequalities for the sumset 2S. Additionally, we explore the converse outcome, finding upper bounds for sets that achieve the best ratio of A^+_k(S) to k, specifically focusing on k equal to 2 and certain instances with k greater than 2.

This study introduces the UniToPatho dataset, comprising 3,557 histopathological fragments tagged with colorectal polyp classification labels and 1,843 regions for adenoma grading. UniToPatho builds upon prior work, notably the Spatially Augmented Histology (SAH) dataset, and addresses its limitations by expanding classification labels to cover not just malignancy, benign, and borderline categories, but also low-grade and high-grade adenomas. Furthermore, UniToPatho enhances grading labels with specific annotations for five distinct adenoma levels. Our innovative approach combines convolutional neural network techniques with multi-task learning, leveraging classification and grading tags to improve overall performance. UniToPatho demonstrates state-of-the-art capability in accurately differentiating healthy tissue from cancerous tissue, achieved through a straightforward Model, while achieving comparable results to top competitors in middle and high-grade adenoma level predictions, and enhancing grading precision with the use of multi-task learning.

We introduce an adjustable finite element method for solving time-harmonic diffusion equations, specifically those with gently varying coefficients in periodically structured domains.  Our new method combines the use of thin element technology and locally refined meshes to efficiently handle high-frequency scenarios.  Key advantages include the elimination of non-physical resonances, robust performance even with highly oscillatory solutions, and minimal reliance on specific scaling parameters.  Our approach enables the creation of accurate and efficient numerical solutions, with a focus on recovering relative errors through mesh refinement.

We contend that recent research oversimplifies water content findings from 4.5 billion years ago, specifically regarding planetesimals in the inner solar system, which are based on analyses of chondrite meteorites. Our argument stems from examining multiple sources of information including enstatite chondrites, petrographic types of chondrite meteorites, and crustal components of terrestrial planets. Our evidence from various perspectives confirms that water content in 4.5 billion year old chondrite particles was significantly higher than previously estimated, likely in excess of 20% by weight, further indicating that water was extensively retained within the primary building blocks of the inner solar system, which is consistent with models suggesting that substantial amounts of water were lost during the differentiation of the planetary bodies that formed from these building blocks.

For the XXZ spin lattice, we obtain finite-lattice correlation functions using the quantum-algebra Bethe-ansatz method. In this work, we derive explicit expressions for the structure factors of higher-spin XXZ lattice models in one dimension. The results demonstrate the affine quantum-group symmetry, which remains intact for all finite-lattice sizes. The obtained expressions for structure factors contain detailed information about the finite-lattice properties, including correlations between distant spins and the effects of anisotropy. Our findings also reveal that certain anisotropy parameters can lead to the isolation of gapless modes in higher-spin chains. These results should provide a useful foundation for exploring finite-lattice properties and isolated gapless modes in one-dimensional integrable higher-spin systems.

In the process of interacting with intelligent systems through voice, a key task is focused on - understanding spoken language. Unlike visual interfaces that are easily comprehended, auditory interactions present more complexities in language grasp. A crucial challenge arises when the system needs to understand language not previously encountered, hindering its effectiveness in dealing with novel inputs. For instance, if a system is trained on dialects of English, it may struggle to understand Welsh dialects. A significant barrier to breaking into the field of natural language processing is the vast amount of data required to train models on new languages. A novel approach has been introduced, allowing voice-based systems to understand any language without prior training, on the condition that the language is written down. A demonstration of this approach has been made by applying it to two distinct voice models, transforming the output in a way that bypasses the need for retraining. The approach has demonstrated the ability to handle voice inputs in two languages the models were not initially trained on, succeeding in over 80% of cases. A key innovation of this approach has been incorporated into two separate voice models, proving its effectiveness. A crucial aspect of this approach has been the use of multiple models that can understand different languages, allowing the system to choose the model best suited to grasp the input language accurately. A significant advancement of this approach has been the elimination of the need to recognize languages, allowing the system to focus solely on understanding the input. We present a comprehensive expansion for electromagnetic scattering and optical force calculations, leveraging the multipoles of an object within a heterogeneous environment. Building on the conventional long wavelength approximation, our approach utilizes the local field concept to optimize calculations for objects with irregular shapes. By accurately assessing electric field variations, our method surpasses the limitations of the long wavelength approximation, enabling a more precise evaluation of scattering and force coefficients. Notably, our approach facilitates the estimation of optical force and torque generated by planar wave propagation in finite thickness media. Interestingly, we find that orthogonality between x and y components of electromagnetic field vectors leads to the isolation of individual torque components. To validate our theory, a numerical analysis is conducted to examine its efficacy in comparison to a rigorous boundary element method.

This study introduces an innovation called quantum immanents for double Schur functions, building on the foundation laid by J.Y. Kim and H. Kim. By leveraging double Young-Capelli bitableaux, specific elements of the algebra $\mathfrak{gl}(n|\mathrm{t}))$, we derive a novel representation for altered Schur functions. Our results also yield new insights into modified Schur functions, encompassing both Kostka-Littlewood vectors in $\mathfrak{gl}(n|\mathrm{t}))$ and their combinatorial descriptions. Furthermore, our approach enables us to define two new families of symmetric functions, demonstrating an intriguing connection to the original Schur functions.

We examine WIMP dark matter within the easiest scoto-seesaw (ESS) framework for neutrino mass generation, investigating how it relates to the naturalness of the Higgs vacuum and consistency with cosmological constraints. TheESS model facilitates a direct link between neutrino and WIMP autonomous creation, allowing us to establish a minimum threshold for the neutrino mass-scale parameter "Lambda" at approximately 10^10 GeV, in line with the model's cosmological effectiveness. Furthermore, we identify suitable parameter regions for the SS heavy doublet masses, finding them to be significantly impacted by the choice of WIMP mass, ranging from approximately 10^3 to 10^5 GeV. Moreover, we find the SS doublet's fifth-dimensional (5D) mass parameter "R" to be distinct from zero, with values ranging from -0.7 to -0.3, influenced by the WIMP mass. Additionally, we find the 5D mass parameter "R" to significantly influence the Higgs vacuum stability, with lower "R" values indicating a need for a more negative "Lambda" value to ensure vacuum stability. Nonetheless, we identify "R" values capable of ensuring vacuum stability at the GUT scale with a standard model Higgs parameter "k" set to 1.2, providing a "technically natural" solution to the Higgs vacuum stability problem.

We employ an $sp^3$ hybridization model to examine its application to 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, with a focus on DFT calculations that incorporate on-site Coulomb interactions. By utilizing a mean-field approximation, we investigate the electronic structure of these materials, particularly the blending of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals in the lower and upper bands of the $d$ shell. Our analysis reveals that this blending causes the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ states, resulting in the distortion of the usual octahedral symmetry and the separation of the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ manifolds. This effect is more pronounced in 5d compounds due to larger hybridization, which may provide a longer-range mechanism for regulating the $d$-band width in these materials.

This study examines how relative quantum homology changes under certain changes in symplectic manifolds, specifically those made by a type of transformation that alters the symplectic form in a controlled manner. We identify specific characteristics of symplectic manifolds that remain unchanged under this transformation, demonstrating this effect using a combination of mathematical techniques. Furthermore, we extend our findings to a related field of study known as topological field theories.

The constant rise in COVID-19 cases necessitates continuous monitoring through frequent chest X-rays, which can strain healthcare systems due to the time-consuming and labor-intensive process of interpreting X-rays by expert radiologists. One potential solution is the use of artificial intelligence in image analysis, which can provide real-time notifications to healthcare professionals about possible illnesses based on changes in X-rays. However, this raises privacy concerns about the storage and sharing of medical images that contain sensitive information about patients. Therefore, modifying chest X-rays to maintain confidentiality while preserving the accuracy of AI-driven illness detection is a crucial issue that this paper aims to address.

ViDaExpert is an innovative tool for creating complex data representations from high-dimensional vector data, specifically designed for user-friendly visualization of large datasets containing up to 200 dimensions and 10000 data points, spanning 5 continuous dimensions and an infinite number of potential features. It offers customizable dimension reductions using user-defined features and automatic clustering in reduced spaces. ViDaExpert facilitates dynamic filtering, sorts data by visual representations, and provides detailed data analysis via an interactive dashboard. Developed for multidimensional vector data analysis, the tool can be used for feature selection, clustering visualization, and complex data visualization.

We determine the number of Newtonian potentials needed to exactly represent a given gravitational field on a flat surface, focusing on scenarios where this representation is possible. By showing that n+1 potentials can always accurately depict a gravitational field defined by n linearly independent data points, we also explore related proof topics. Additionally, we investigate conditions under which unique combinations of these potentials can be achieved. These findings have implications for the broader theory of potential theory within R^n space.
